sections.title: 1. Purpose of
sections.content:
The provision of this Section of the Act is utterly misused. The real benefit of the said Section does not go to the weakest and meekest among Scheduled Cast. The really weak and poor people of Scheduled Caste do not encroach upon the Gaon Sabha land and only strong and influential persons of Scheduled Caste (which may be described as creamy layer) can forcibly occupy Gaon Sabha land. Moreover, whenever a new cutoff date is provided, unscrupulous and influential persons of scheduled cast manufacture evidence of their prior possession and in this regard Lekhpals and Pradhans sometimes provide full support to them. Sanjai Kumar vs. Collector/District Magistrate , 2005 (1) RD 454: 2005 (3) AWC 2622see also Ghanshyam Singh vs. State of U.P., 2005 (1) RD 489: 2005 (3) AWC 1040 (para 7)
The jurisdiction to prevent damage, misappropriation and wrongful occupation of gram panchayat property vests in the authority described under Section 67 of the Code. Consequently, the appropriate remedy available to the Gram Sabha was to invoke the provisions of Section 67 of the Code or the erstwhile provisions of Section 122B of the U.P.Z.A. & L.R. Act. Jahar Singh vs. State of U.P. , PIL No 32892 of 2016, decided on 31.01.2017, (per J. SP Kesarwani)

sections.title: 2. Scope of
sections.content: This section being a non-obstante clause, is an exception to normal rule that Gaon Sabha land cannot be settled nor can be allotted otherwise than in accordance with relevant provisions of law nor can be allowed to remain in possession or occupation of any person unless allotted by means of lease/Patta, granted under the provisions framed under the Act and Rules. Shambhoo Nath vs. Commissioner, 2007 (102) RD 136: 2007 (5) AWC 4984 (ref. para 9)

sections.title: 3. Scope and Applicability of
sections.content: This Section carves out an exception which permits the occupation over the Gaon Sabha land by certain class of persons namely Scheduled Caste/Scheduled tribe, an agricultural labourer and has been in possession over the said land since before May 1, 2002. This provision appears to have been made looking to the interest of the scheduled caste or scheduled tribe persons, who are agricultural labourer. Shambhoo Nath vs. The Commissioner, Vindhyachal, 2007 (102) RD 136 (ref para 14)

sections.title: 4. Benefit under 122-B
sections.content:
Entitled to get only if he can show that his name entered in revenue records as occupant before 1-5-2002. This apart they are also not entitled for benefit of Section 123(1) as it is clearly emerged that they have not build their house prior to 1.5.2002. Satya Veer vs. State of U.P., 2015 (4) AWC 3557see also Ghanshyam Singh vs. State of U.P., 2005 (98) RD 489
No formal declaration is required when the benefit is to be extended to a person who had been in possession from before a cut-off date provided under the provision. Such villager becomes as Asankrmaniya Bhumidhar automatically. If two villagers or individuals claim right over the land then they had to approach the proper Court of competent jurisdiction. Berendra and another vs. State of U.P Through Secretary (Revenue and Finance), Lucknow and others, 2018(141) RD 589

sections.title: 5. Widowed agricultural labourer
sections.content: Section 122-B does not provide for any special or additional rights to widowed agricultural labourer belonging to Schedule Caste or Scheuled Tribe. Raj Kumar vs. Rajswa Parishad U.P., 2010 (4) AWC 3779

sections.title: 6. Procedure under
sections.content:
This Section provides for the mode and procedure for taking action with regard to property vested in the Gaon Sabha or local authority, which is damaged or misappropriated. Sub-section (4F) has been substituted to save certain category of persons, namely, agricultural labourer belonging to Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe from the aforesaid action if he is in occupation of the Gaon Sabha property since before a particular date. Brahmi vs. District Magistrate/DDC, 2002 RD 393:2002 (3) AWC 1848 (para 10)
Proceedings under the Section are of summary in nature and if the Gaon Sabha being party to suit and if it is decreed in under with law, order passed would be a nullity and binding on both the parties.Thakur Prasad vs. Upper Collector, Gorakhpur, 2001 RD 116

sections.title: 7. Cryptic Order
sections.content: Chief Revenue Officer has no authority to pass cryptic order along with order for claiming of damages without reasonable and seasoned grounds. Jaypati vs. Chief Revenue Officer, Allahabad, 2001 RD 715: 2003 (3) AWC 2379

sections.title: 8. Benefit can be assailed by filing suit
sections.content: Held, benefits of provisions under section 122-B (4-F) can only be availed on filling a regular suit under section 28 of the Act.Dalle vs. Parjee, 2001 (1) AWC 26 (H): 2000 RD 71 (BR)

sections.title: 9. Assistant Collector**jurisdiction of
sections.content:
The provisions of sub-section (2) of section 122-B confer jurisdiction on the Assistant Collector only when the disputed land is prima facie proved to be the Gaon Sabha property. It should be established that the land had, at some time vested in Gaon Sabha. Action is permissible only when the title of the Gaon Sabha cannot be ex-facie questioned. Laxmi Dhar vs. State of U.P., 1987 RD 87
Assistant Collector had exclusive jurisdiction to exercise power to prevent damage, misappropriation and wrongful occupation of any encroachment over Gram Panchayat property. Jahar Singh v. State of U.P. and others, 2017 (3) AWC 3177

sections.title: 10. Assistant Collector**powers of
sections.content:
The Explanation given under Section 122B (4F) provides that for the purpose of section the expression “Collector” means officer appointed as Collector under the provisions of U.P. Land Revenue Act, 1901 and includes Additional Collector. Assistant Collector was not entitled to grant the benefit to any person under Section 122B (4F) of the Act.Shiv Raj vs. Additonal Collector, 1998 (1) 730 (para 9)
The Assistant Collector has to satisfy that there is misappropriation of property but first of all the authority concerned has to record the findings that the property has been vested in the Gaon Sabha under the provisions of the Act. Kala vs. Collector, Haridwar, 2005 (2) RD 360 (Utt)
Assistant Collector has been enjoined to satisfy on these points for application of Section 122B, viz., (a) whether the property is vested under the provisions of Act in Gaon Sabha or the collector, (b) whether the property is damaged or misappropriated, (c) whether the Gaon Sabha or local authority is entitled to have or retain possession of any land under provisions of Act and (d) whether the land has been occupied otherwise than in accordance with law under the provisions of the Act. Meharwan vs. Collector, 2006 (1) AWC 509 (para 5&6)

sections.title: 11. Property
sections.content: The word ‘property’ used in section 122-B (1) is wide enough to include even water of a tank or talab, and if such water is misappropriated by any person, damages can be awarded under the said provision. Sheo Dayal vs. Gaon Sabha, 1981 RJ 61

sections.title: 12. Consolidation of Holdings Act
sections.content: Land contributed for a public purpose under the Consolidation of Holdings Act also comes within the purview of this Section. Tula Ram vs. Gram Samaj, 1982 RD 237

sections.title: 13. Show cause notice
sections.content: The provision regarding show cause notice is dealt within sub-section (2) to (4). The notice to the occupant has to be issued in the prescribed form. Banshidhar vs. Gaon Sabha, 1999 RD 19 (Hindi). Such a notice has to be issued in Form 49-A, notice to a dead person is illegal. Phatai vs. Kharpattu, 1992 RD 169 (Supp)

sections.title: 14. Compensation**conditions applicable
sections.content:
While awarding compensation for damage, the Assistant Collector should bear in mind two important factors
firstly, the date of compensation should be in accordance with Rules 115F of Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Rules, 1951 and secondly, that the amount of compensation should not be more than one mentioned in the notice in Form 49-A of the Rules. Shilta Dean vs. Gaon Sabha, 1979 AWC (Rev) 65. It has been held that the market value of the land cannot be made on the basis of the compensation under this Section. Lutawan vs. Gaon Sabha, 1983 RD 281

sections.title: 15. Wrongful occupation
sections.content: In case of a wrongful occupation, the compensation should be assessed at 100 times of the amount of rent calculated at the sanctioned hereditary rates. Rati Ram vs. Tahsildar, 1992 RD 474. The damages for award of amount of compensation cannot exceed the amount underlined in Form 49-KA. Pratap Singh vs. State of U.P., 2005 (1) RD 772: 2005 (3) UPLBEC 2639

sections.title: 16. Benefit under 122B(4F)
sections.content:
The benefit of Section 122-B (4F) can be granted to only those agricultural labourers, who belongs to Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe. If the petitioner belonged to Kathera caste, he must prove that such caste is included in the category of Scheduled Caste.Netrapal vs. Additional Collector, 1999 RD 405.
The benefit under Section 122B (4F) is available only in respect of land vested in Gaon Sabha and does not extend to land vested in the State or in any other authority apart from Gaon Sabha.Rameshwar vs. Deputy Director of Consolidation, 2002 RD 475: 2002 (3) AWC 2328 (para 8)
Application for granting benefit hereunder Section 122-B (4F) is not independently maintainable. Sameer Das vs. State of U.P., 2012 (115) RD 705 (para 13)
Whenever a new cutoff date for conferring benefit of Section 122-B (4-F) of the Act is provided, people belonging to scheduled caste start claiming benefit of the said Section by creating evidence of prior possession. In view of this rampant mal-practice it is most essential that whenever benefit of aforesaid sub-section (4-F) is claimed the claimant must show that he is in unauthorized possession over Gaon Sabha land and his name is recorded in the revenue records prior to the cutoff date or the proceedings for his ejectment must be pending since before the cutoff date. If it is not so then no amount of evidence can be looked into in that regard. In most of the cases like the present ones Pradhans, Lekhpals and other Revenue authorities in collusion with claimants give wrong reports of possession of the claimants prior to the cutoff date” Ghanshyam Singh vs. State of UP, 2010 (5) AWC 4651
In order to claim benefit under the Section, essential ingredients that must be proved are, firstly he is in unauthorised possession over Gaon Sabha land and his name is recorder in Revenue Records prior to the cutoff date or ejectment proceedings pending before the cutoff date. Sanjai Kumar vs. Collector/District Magistrate, Kanpur Dehat, 2005 (1) RD 454: 2005 (3) AWC 2622 see also Ghanshyam Singh vs. State, 2005 (1) RD 489: 2005 (3) AWC 1040 (para 3).
The provision gives protection to the possession of a person belonging to the scheduled caste and scheduled tribe from any action under Section 122B. Moreover the benefit of Section 122B (4F) can only be claimed when the land is vested in the Gaon Sabha under Section 117. Shivnath vs. A.D.J., 2005 (1) AWC 808 (para 9)
Person entitled to get benefit hereunder shall be admitted as a bhumidhar with non-transferable rights of land under Section 195 and it shall not be necessary to get declaration to that effect. Reshma Devi vs. Commissioner, 2014 (1) RD 677 (para 8)

sections.title: 17. Applicability of
sections.content: For a person to be admitted as Bhumidhar under Section 122-B of the Act, the two main conditions that has to be satisfied are, firstly he should prove that he is an agricultural labourer and secondly, to show his main source of livelihood is through agricultural labour. Kripal Singh vs. State of U.P., 2005 (2) RD 597 see also Munna Lal vs. Additional Commissioner (Administration), Kanpur, 2005 (99) RD 141

sections.title: 18. Scope of 122-B (4F)
sections.content: Section 122-B (4F) specifically provides that no right under this Section shall accrue on lands specified in Section 132, because they are lands of public utility. Maya Devi vs. Additional Commissioner, 1999 RD 775. The same would be the case of graveyard. Tej Singh vs. Gaon Sabha, 1986 RD 86. In one case the land was set apart for deosthan during consolidation proceedings and the claim under Section 122 (4F) was neglected. Babu Nandan vs. Board of Revenue, Allahabad, 1993 RD 195. But despite the above decision, the Board of Revenue, held in one case that Section 132 does not override Section 122-B (4F) and the benefit of the later provision can be granted on land covered by Section 132 of the Act. Gaon Sabha vs. Chief Revenue Officer, 1997 RD 7 (H)

sections.title: 19. Section 122-B(4F) and Section 132
sections.content: Law is very clear that neither any Bhumidhari right nor any right under Section 122B (4F) of UP Z. A. and L. R. Act could accrue in any land mentioned under Section 132. Ram Singh vs. Deputy Director, Consolidation, 2004 (1) RD157: 2004 (1) AWC 687 (para 5)

sections.title: 20. Recovery proceedings
sections.content: Question with regards to litigation between petitioner’s father and Gaon Sabha not dealt with by the Courts below before passing order of recovery of damages. Matter remanded back to Additional Collector to record fresh findings. Kala vs. Collector, Haridwar, 2005 (2) RD (Utt HC): 2005 (2) UD 335: 2006 (1) UC 535

sections.title: 21. Navin Parti land
sections.content:
The land admittedly recorded as Navin Parti and was owned by the Gram Sabha. The Pradhan of the village had no authority to give the said land to the petitioner or anybody else. The whole transaction entered into between the parties was wholly illegal and without jurisdiction. Ambika Prasad vs. Collector, Sitapur, 2002 RD 172: 2002 AWC (2) 1720 (para 5&6)
Disputed land, recorded as ‘Navin Patri’ which is not fit for cultivation, but entry in khasra shows petitioners had sown wheat in the said plot. Court held that to convert a banjar land into cultivable is not only desirable but also essential. Instead of eviction petitioners should pay damages equivalent to market value in lieu of land. Land vests with the petitioner. Kishore Singh vs. Additional Collector, Agra, 2007 (2) RD 210 (para 3&4)see also Mannoo Prasad vs.Upper Collector, (Prashan) Kanpur Dehat, 2008 (105) RD

sections.title: 22. Encroachment**imposition of fine
sections.content: On local inspection of disputed land it is found to have encroachment and illegal construction upon them. Hence, order of ejectment and imposition of fine is not illegal. Ahmed Ali vs. Additional Collector, Muzaffarnagar, 2002 RD 545

sections.title: 23. Unauthorized occupant
sections.content:
There shall be no entertainment of application by person who seeks protection of rights as sub-section (1) to (3) of Section 122-B empowers of Assistant Collector to initiate action on basis of information received by him to put an end to misuse or unauthorized occupation of property belonging to Gaon Sabha or a local authority. Monorey @ Manohar vs. Board of Revenue, 2003 (5) AWC 4441 (SC): 2003 (1) RD 538.
No one can be allowed to take illegal possession of the Gaon Sabha land and if any one makes such an attempt, the State should stop it. Chob Singh vs. State of U.P., 2000 RD 233:2000 (39) ALR 358: 2000 (2) AWC 877 (para 6)

sections.title: 24. Judicial proceedings
sections.content: The proceedings under Section 122-B have judicial complexion though are not at par with civil suit, still such proceedings do not detract from merit of being judicial proceedings, as legislature have empowered an Assistant Collector with all powers like issuance of notice, receiving of objection and adducing evidence from the parties.Meharwan vs. Collector, Kanpur Dehat, 2005 (2) RD 427: 2006 (1) AWC 509: 2005 (3) ACJ 2166

sections.title: 25. Tahsildar**powers of
sections.content: Assumption of powers to initiate proceedings by Tahsildar are wholly without jurisdiction and illegal and liable to be quashed. Kali Charan vs. Additional Collector, 2005 (2) RD 801: 2006 (1) AWC 813: 2006 (1) LCD 97 (para 8)

sections.title: 26. Eviction or imposition of damages
sections.content:
If a person is in possession for more than 12 years, instead of eviction award of damage is the appropriate relief. In view of this, even though the validity of allotment was not fully proved by the petitioner still due to inordinate delay of 30 years in initiating the proceedings for eviction, award of the damages is the appropriate relief instead of eviction. Shyam Deo vs. Collector, 2003 (1) RD 700 (para 3) see also Bhudaee vs. Collector 2005 (98) RD 741, D.C.M. Ltd. vs. Collector, 2007 (7) AWC 7138
Both the Courts below have grossly erred in holding that the petitioner was in unauthorized and illegal occupation of the land in question merely on the basis of surmises and conjectures and also committed error apparent on the face of the record by arriving at a conclusion on the statement of the Lekhpal that the petitioner was in unauthorized occupation whereas as per record the Lekhpal himself had stated that he had no knowledge of any such unauthorized occupation.Deo Narain vs. Addl. Collector, 2006 (1) AWC 433

sections.title: 27. Limitation**Effect of
sections.content: There is no limitation to initiate the proceedings by Gaon Sabha for eviction of persons who are in unauthorised occupation of its land. Shyam Deo vs. Collector, 2003 (1) RD 700 (para 3) see also Bhudaee vs. Collector, 2005 (98) RD 741

sections.title: 28. Imposition of damages
sections.content: Petitioner illegally and unauthorisedly fell down standing trees from the land that belongs to Gaon Sabha, therefore the damages imposed on him by the Collector does not require interference in revision. Ram Kishore vs. District Magistrate, Fatehpur, 2003 (2) RD 440

sections.title: 29. On-spot inspection
sections.content: Petitioner vehemently denied that he is in possession of the disputed land, in view of legal position and G.O. of 1975 which states that no fine can be imposed if possession denied, order imposing fine unsustainable. Regarding eviction, matter remanded back to Additional Collector with direction to have on spot inspection before passing any order. Hukum Singh vs. Tehsildar (Upper/Assistant Collector) Roorkee, 2005 (2) RD 446 (Utt)

sections.title: 30. Procedure under
sections.content: Revision is not barred under Section 122-B (4-A) and the aggrieved person has a statutory right to challenge order passed by Authority under Section 122-B of the Act. The remedy if such can be availed by him but after filing revision he cannot file such as proved in Section 122-B (4-E). But on that accord revision will not become maintainable.Bahadur vs. Additional Collector, Agra, 2005 (1) RD 743 (para 7)

sections.title: 31. Plea of res judicata
sections.content: Under Section 122-B and Rule 115 proceeding was initiated by Gaon Sabha and LMC against petitioner for eviction. The impugned order was quashed against which appeal was allowed. But the Board of Revenue set aside the appeal, second appeal instituted. Held, no res judicata lies for order passed under Section 122B, therefor petition dismissed. Smt. Shakuntala vs. Board of Revenue, 2006 (2) RD 713

sections.title: 32. Disposition of
sections.content: The petitioner cannot be disposed from his land even if date of vesting in occupation on Gaon Sabha got changed from 30.06.1985 to 01.05.2002. Panchu vs. Collector, Gorakhpur, 2006 (2) RD 562

sections.title: 33. Aggrieved person
sections.content:
Application under Section 122B will not be maintainable if the respondents are not aggrieved person and Gaon Sabha land under prescribed authority found that petitioner had not encroached the land. Gulab Chand vs. State of U.P., 2007 (6) RD ADJ 224
The expression ‘aggrieved person’ denotes an elastic and an elusive concept. It cannot be confined within the bounds of a rigid, exact and comprehensive definition. Its scope and meaning depends on diverse, variable factors such as the content and intent of the statute of which contravention is alleged, the specific circumstances of the case, the nature and extent of complainant’s interest and the nature and the extent of the prejudice or injury suffered by the complainant. Subhash Babu v. State of A.P., AIR 2011 SC 3031

sections.title: 34. Recall application
sections.content: Powers to revision against an order rejecting recall application for order passed under Section 122-B of the Act lies with the Collector under sub-section (4A) of the Act. Rajveer Singh vs. Collector, Ghaziabad, 2002 (93) RD 399 (para 9)

sections.title: 35. Revisional Order
sections.content: Held, Civil suit against revisional order of Collector challenging order of Assistant Collector under Section 122-B (4D) is maintainable.Rajendra Singh vs. State of U.P., 2008 (4) AWC 3310

sections.title: 36. Initiation of proceedings without resolution
sections.content: Pradhan initiated proceedings u/s 122B without a resolution of Land Management Committee as envisaged under the Act, nor was Assistant Collector informed about the same. Order is unsustainable. Kali Charan vs. Additional Collector, Azamgarh, 2005 (2) RD 801

sections.title: 37. Sanctioned Hereditary Rates
sections.content: Damages must be ascertained in accordance to sanctioned Hereditary Rates as defined under Section 110 to 112 of U.P. Tenancy Act. J.K. Dairy and Foods Ltd. vs. ADM (F&R), 2007 (1) RD 375: 2007 (2) AWC 1715

sections.title: 38. Summary proceedings
sections.content: Since proceedings under this Section are summary in nature, provisions of review are not available. Chief Revenue Officer not confirmed with jurisdiction of review and reopening of matters. Keshav Tiwari vs. C.R.O, Ballia, 2009 (108) RD

sections.title: 39. Allotment made under Consolidation Act
sections.content: The provisions of Section 122B (4F) are not applicable on a land on which petitioner is in possession in pursuance of allotment made under the U. P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, by virtue of the allotment he is in possession of the land and his possession and title over the land till said allotment survives cannot be said unauthorised possession. Brahmi vs. District Magistrate/DDC, 2002 RD 393:2002 (3) AWC 1848 (para 11)

sections.title: 40. Entry in Revenue Records
sections.content: There is no bar against an application being made by the eligible person coming within the four corners of sub-section (4F) to effect necessary changes in the revenue record. Whence the claim of the applicant is accepted, it is the bounden duty of the concerned revenue authorities to make necessary entries in revenue records to give effect to the statutory mandate. Manorey alias Manohar vs. Board of Revenue, 2003 AIR 4102: 2003 (5 ) SCC 521: 2003 (3) JT 538: 2003 (5) AWC 4441: 2003 RD 538 (SC)

sections.title: 41. When cannot be evicted
sections.content: If the occupant of the land satisfies the conditions under sub-section (4F) then he shall not be evicted by taking recourse to sub-Section (1) to (3) of Section 122B and he is endowed with the rights of a bhumidhar with non transferable rights. Manorey alias Manohar vs. Board of Revenue, 2003 AIR 4102: 2003 (5 ) SCC 521: 2003 (3) JT 538: 2003 (5) AWC 4441: 2003 RD 538 (SC)

sections.title: 42. Plea of adverse possession
sections.content: Petitioners contention that the proceedings initiated under Section 122B of the U.P.Z.A. and L.R. Act read with Rule 115D of the U.P.Z.A. and L.R. Rules having been dropped, the petitioners have perfected their title over the plot by adverse possession, holds no ground as these are summary proceedings which are initiated by a notice and are tried by a Tahsildar, there could be no declaration of title of any person in these proceedings. Likhi Ram alias Moola vs. State of UP, 2002 RD 126: 2002 (1) AWC 521 (DB)(para 13)

sections.title: 43. Ejectment order not challenged**effect of
sections.content: Against the order passed by the trial court for ejectment and imposing damages, the petitioner did not file any revision. Hence, the said order, therefore, became final and the petitioner now has no right to challenge the same under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. Ambika Prasad vs. Collector, Sitapur, 2003 RD 172: 2002 (2) AWC 1720 (par 8)

sections.title: 44. Trespass
sections.content: In view of the facts that the land was allotted to petitioner by the Land Management Committee and on the basis of which the petitioner occupied the land and raised constructions, the petitioner cannot be held to be trespasser or a person in unauthorised occupation of Gram Sabha property. The proceedings initiated against him under Section 122B of the Act were, therefore, misconceived and the orders impugned in the writ petition, are liable to be quashed. Abhay Raj Singh vs. Upper Ziladhikari (Prashashan), 1999 RD 24: 1999 (2) AWC 938 (para 6)

sections.title: 45. Adjudication of title in land**whether a dispute of civil nature
sections.content: It may be noticed here that the dispute springing from consolidation is a state sponsored dispute as to title pertaining agricultural land. No court other than the consolidation courts, not even the apex court, can entertain any matter relating to cause of action arising out of consolidation area of such litigation. Therefore, it leaves no manner of doubt the consolidation courts are the courts deciding the civil rights relating to agricultural land. Chandra Bhan vs. DDC, 2006 (1) RD 268 (para 31)

sections.title: 46. Order under 122B can be challenged
sections.content: Order under Section 122B of the Act can be challenged in a suit under sub-section (4D) of Section 122B of the Act. If a revision is filed, suit is barred. But the order in revision can be challenged in suit in view of sub-section (4E) of Section 122B of the Act. Disputed question of fact can best be decided in a suit which is an appropriate remedy and writ cannot be maintained. Kajoda vs. Assistant Collector, Finance and Revenue Mathura, 1996 (2) AWC 1042 :1996 ACJ 620 relied and referred in Kali Charan vs. Additional District Magistrate, 2000 (2) AWC 1669

sections.title: 47. River-bed**Allotment of
sections.content:
The petitioner being a landless Harijan (Pasi) cannot be given benefit of Section 122B (4F) of the U. P. Z. A. and L. R. Act as the said land is in the nature of ‘talab’ and land covered by water cannot be allowed to be given in the bhumidhari right to the petitioner. Chhotey Lal vs. Addl. (Upper) Collector, 2004 (2) RD 149: 2004 (3) AWC 2649 (para 10).
No protection is available to person who is possessing land covered under Section 132 of the Act. Jai Singhs vs. State of Uttaranchal, 2009 (2) UD 585.
No relief can be granted with respect to land covered under Section 132 of the Act.Ram Jivan vs. Additional Commissioner, 2014 (124) RD 219

sections.title: 48. Bhumidhari rights
sections.content: When Sub-section (4-F) categorically and lucidly says that a person, who is covered by the said provision will not have to seek declaration by filing a suit and he/she would be admitted as bhumidhar with non-transferable rights under Section 195, suit for declaration, itself was not maintainable, as was superfluous litigation.Shambhoo Nath vs. Commissioner, 2007 (102) RD 136: 2007 (5) AWC 4984

sections.title: 49. Civil Suit**Maintainability of
sections.content: Civil suit challenging revisional order of Collector against order of Assistant Collector is maintainable.Rajendra Singh vs. State of U.P., 2008 (4) AWC 3310

sections.title: 50. Asami lease holder
sections.content: Section 122-B (4F) cannot be interpreted to mean that holder of asami lease are conferred with non-transferable bhumidhari rights.

sections.title: 51. Revision
sections.content: Revision hereunder can only be maintainable if the suit is filed on grounds mentioned under clauses (a) to (c) of Section 333 of the Act, which is para materia with Section 15 of Code of Civil Procedure.Pooran Chandra vs. Collector, 2005 (2) UD 704 (Utt): 2006 (3) UC 1495

sections.title: 52. Public Utility Land
sections.content:
Land covered by the provisions of Section 132 of the Act could not be granted to anybody since the land is a public utility land.Zahir vs. Additional Collector, 2007 (2) UD 396: 2008 (1) UC 275 (Utt HC)
Petitioner in possession of public utility land i.e. goher/rasta is not entitled to any relief or protection.Jai Singh vs. State of Uttarakhand, 2010 (1) UAD 379 (Utt)

sections.title: 53. Alternate remedy
sections.content:
Where petitioner has an alternate remedy by filing suit before court of competent jurisdiction this writ petition is not maintainableAngoor vs. State of U.P., 2012 (117) RD 387see also Birbal vs. Additional Comm, 2012 (117) RD 395.
A Division Bench of Allahabad High Court in Rajendra Singh vs. State of U.P. and others, (2008) 6 ADJ 386 wherein it has been held that in the proceedings arising under Section 122-B of the Act, there is an alternative and efficacious remedy by way of suit whether the order is passed by Assistant Collector or Collector but a writ petition is not maintainable.
The order passed under Section 67 of U.P. Revenue Code, 2006 was held to be appealable under sub-section (5) and in view thereof, the petition filed by the person aggrieved from the order of Assistant Collector was dismissed as not maintainable, on the ground of availability of statutory alternative remedy. Thus, Allahabad High Court was of the considered view that the appeal filed by the petitioners was maintainable and has illegally been dismissed as not maintainable on the ground that the petitioners were not party in the proceedings. Peer Mohammad vs. State of U.P. and others (Writ Petition No. 13397 (MB) of 2020, decided on 28.08.2020)

sections.title: 54. Condonation of delay
sections.content: Though the ecplanation furnished by the petitioner for delay in filing an appeal even then such orders must not have been passed and delay should have been condoned after imposition of fine.Dodram vs. Collector, 2014 (4) RD333 (para 16)

sections.title: 55. Ex-parte order
sections.content: Since petitioner has been entended benefit of Section 122-B (4-F) on the basis of report of revenue authorities and petitioner acquired bhumidhari rights (non-transferable) his name cannot be expunged from Revenue Records by an ex-parte order.Ram Babu vs. State of U.P., 2014 (4) RD 362 (para 7)

sections.title: 56. Summary suit
sections.content: Held, once order has been passed in the summary proceeding the remedy of petitioner lies in filing civil suit and such question decided in summary proceedings are subject to suit.Rajendra Singh vs. State of U.P. 2008 (4) AWC 3310

sections.title: 57. Asami lease**determination of
sections.content: It is true that an asami lease cannot be determined in proceedings under section 122-B which provides for eviction of unauthorized occupants. A person recorded as an asami cannot be said to be an unauthorized occupant especially when entry not alleged to be a forged or fraudulent. Baijanath (D) vs. State of U.P., 2016 (132) RD 294

sections.title: 58. Encroachment over Gaon Sabha land –ejectment proceedings maintainable
sections.content: In the instant case, Court finds that there is nothing to indicate that Gaon Sabha was divested of its rights or that the rights of the Gaon Sabha was resumed by any notification issued by the State. Neither, there is an indication that a notification under Section 117(3) and 117(6) had been issued declaring that the plot in question has been transferred to another local body. Merely by extending territorial limits would not divest or resume the proprietary rights of Gaon Sabha unless there is a notification to that effect under Section 117 of the Act. Hence, held that the Gaon Sabha continued to exercise its right and perform its functions. Ejectment proceedings initiated under Section 122-B was maintainable. Rameshwar Prasad vs. Tahsildar/Assistant Collector, Moradabad, 2010(1) ALJ 464

sections.title: 59. Assessment of damages
sections.content: The provision of S. 115-F(2) makes it specifically clear that in case of wrongful occupation of land, the damage caused to the Gaon Sabha or the local authority, as the case may be, shall be assessed for each year of such wrongful occupation or any part thereof, at 100 times the amount of rent computed at the sanctioned hereditary rates applicable to the plots concerned. M/s. J.K. Dairy and Foods Ltd. (Chhoya) Gajraula through It s Vice President vs. Additional District Magistrate (F & R)/Upper Collector, Jyotiba Phule Nagar and Others, 2007 (102) RD 375

sections.title: 60. Injunction Suit**Jurisdiction of
sections.content: The principle laid down in Ram Awalamb and others vs. Jata Shanker and others 1968 RD 470 (FB) will apply also to a suit for injunction and demolition relating to agricultural land and brought against a trespasser. Where the revenue court was not competent to grant all the reliefs arising out of one and the same cause of action and the main relief was that of injunction and demolition the suit would lie in the civil court.” In the instant case only one relief of injunction has been sought so the civil court has jurisdiction to decide the suit. State of U.P. vs. Ram Prasad Saxena, 2013 (2) ALJ 38

sections.title: 61. Permanent injunction**Abadi land
sections.content: Eviction orders passed by Assistant Collector confirmed in revision, hence, possession of plaintiff-petitioners prima facie illegal – No case for grant of temporary injunction made out. Property descriebe in Section 117 of U.P.Z.A. and L.R. Act includes abadi sites.Bhagwana Singh vs. Gaon Sabha Village Paijaniya, Bijnor, 2006(2) AWC 1684

sections.title: 62. Admission as Bhumidhar with non-transferable rights–When could be made
sections.content: The provisions contained under Section 122-B (4-F) of the Act are deeming provisions and it provides for conferring rights of a Bhumidhar with non-transferable rights who is in possession over the land under Section 195 of the Act, if he is found in possession prior to 13th May, 2007 and no separate proceedings are required to be initiated for claiming such rights.Shambhoo Nath vs. Commissioner, Vindhyachal Region, Mirzapur, 2007 (102) RD 136

sections.title: 63. Protection from eviction**power of judicial review
64. Proceedings under Section 67**procedure under
sections.content: Proceedings under Section 67(a) of the Code should be registered immediately after a defence in that regard is made in proceedings under Section 67 of the Code. The proceedings under Sections 67 and 67(a) of the Code, should be consolidated and heard together by the same Court. Such procedure would faithfully implement the legislative intent and also serve the interest of justice. The Courts in proceedings under Section 67 Code are under obligation of law to decide the eligibility of the notice for protection under Section 67(a) Code, in case such defence is tendered by the notice. The said proceedings shall be registered separately. But both cases will be consolidated and heard and decided together. Asgar vs. State of U.P. and others, 2021(8) ADJ 313 see also Baburam vs. State of U.P. and others, 2021(8) ADJ 100

sections.title: 65. Who can maintain Appeal
sections.content: A bare reading of sub-section (5) shows that any ‘person’ may be the ‘party’ or may not be a party can maintain an appeal if he is aggrieved from the order of the Assistant Collector under sub section (3) or sub section (4). Sub section (5), therefore, is not confined to party aggrieved from the order passed under sub-section (3) or sub-section (4) of Section 67, but also includes a non-party to the proceedings if he can show that he is a ‘person aggrieved’ from the order passed under sub section (3) or sub section (4). Ghanshyam Verma and others vs. State of U.P. and others, 2021(7) ADJ 67(LB).

sections.title: 66. Encroachments over land
sections.content: The earlier proceedings, under Section 122­B of the Z.A. Act, drawn against the petitioner’s father, having been dropped upon his death, and there being no adjudication on merits, and the fresh report submitted by the Area Lekhpal, on the basis of a spot inspection, being indicative of encroachments over the land in question by the petitioner, there would be no bar to initiation of fresh proceedings under Section 67 of the Revenue Code. Mukesh Pachauri vs. State of UP and 3 others, 2024:AHC:147848

sections.title: 67. Filling of Writ Petition for Resolution of LMC**mandatory
sections.content: As the writ petition was filed by the Gram Pradhan without there being any resolution of the Land Management Committee or the Gaon Sabha, the same was not maintainable. Gram Sabha Komna Balrampur vs. Deputy Director of Consolidation Balrampur, 2020 R.D. 512

sections.title: 68. Illegal encroachment on Gaon Sabha land**Eviction order**Sustainability of
sections.content: When the impugned eviction order was passed without making proper survey/demarcation of plot in question, such an order is not liable to be sustained, hence set aside and matter remanded back with certain directions. It was further directed that if the proceeding under Section 67 of U.P. Revenue Code, 2006 is decided in favour of the petitioners, the petitioner’s construction which had been demolished in arbitrary manner by the State authority shall be reconstructed accordingly. Ashok Kumar vs. State of U.P., 2023 (160) RD 726

sections.title: 69. Encroachment on public pond**Removal of Consideration
sections.content:
Herein, encroachment over pond has neither been intimated by the Land Management Committee nor by the Lekhpal and the petitioner if filed an application informing the authority regarding such encroachment, the application of the petitioner, in Court’s considered opinion, shall be covered under the umbrella of the world ‘otherwise’ used in Section 67 (2) & Rule 67 of the Rules. Bhola Nath and another v. State of U.P. and others, 2016 (6) AWC 6363
70. Disputes regarding boundaries–Powers of District Magistrate–In our Constitution, there is clear separation of judicial and executive powers. The civil disputes are to be decided by the Civil Court and unsuccessful litigant has a right to file an appeal. The Administrative Officials cannot enter into any such dispute in exercise of the power conferred on them under the provisions of CrPC and the Revenue Code to fill in the gap and pass executive orders which explicitly belongs to the realms of Civil Court or the revenue court respectively. The due process of law has to be followed in all respect and the executive authorities are not supposed usurp the power bestowed on the civil/revenue courts as it would not only be exercise of excessive jurisdiction not permissible under law but would also lead to overlapping jurisdiction which is against the tenets of the basic structure of our Constitution. Vijai vs. State of U.P. and others, 2022 AIR CC 3254 (All)

sections.title: 71. Functions of Sub-Divisional Officer and Commissioner **Nature of
sections.content:
The Sub-Divisional Officer, acting under sub-section (1) of Section 24, is empowered to “decide” any “dispute” regarding boundaries, and the order passed by the Sub-Divisional Officer is subject to any appeal under sub-section (4) before the Commissioner, the order of the Commissioner thereafter is to be final. The provisions contained sub-section (1) and sub-section (4) of Section 24 leave no room for doubt that the Sub-Divisional Officer and also the Commissioner exercising powers thereunder, discharge judicial functions. Jhinka Devi vs. State of U.P. and ors., 2022 (7) ADJ 31
Rule 67 (6) of the U P Revenue Code Rules, 2006 mandates that the Assistant Collector shall conclude the enquiry under Section 67 within 90 days of the issuance of the show cause notice and in case of failure to adhere to the time frame, the authority is obliged to record reasons. Dayaram Yadav and others vs. State of U.P. through Chief Secretary, U.P. Govt., Lucknow, 2016 (6) ADJ 275: 2016 (132) RD 11 see also Om Prakash Varma vs. State of U.P., 2014 (5) ADJ 427 (DB)(LB)

sections.title: 71[67A. Certain house sites to be settled with existing owners thereof
sections.content:
71 Inserted vide U.P. Act No. 4 of 2016 w.e.f. 16.12.2015
(1) If any person referred to in sub-section (1) of Section 64 has built a house on any land referred to in Section 63 of this Code, not being land reserved for any public purpose, and such house exists on the November 29, 2012, the site of such house shall be held by the owner of the house on such terms and conditions as may be prescribed.
(2) Where any person referred to in sub-section (1) of Section 64, has built a house on any land held by a tenure holder (not being a government lessee) and such house exists on November 29, 2000, the site of such house, notwithstanding anything contained in this Code, be deemed to be settled with the owner of such house by the tenure holder on such terms and conditions as may be prescribed.

sections.content: Availability of

sections.title: 1. Nature of
sections.content: The provision of Section 123(2), as amended from time to time, was only prospective in nature and could not be given a retrospective effect. Majid vs. Rahmatullah, 2007 (102) RD 235 see also Rameshwar Gond vs. IInd Addl. District Judge, Deoria, RD 1998 (89) 742

sections.title: 2. Scope of
sections.content: The provision of Section 123(2) of the Act does not give any overriding effect to any valid decree passed by a court of law. In fact, the expression “notwithstanding anything contained in the Act” as given in the Section is confined only to the provisions Zamindari Act. Vishwanath vs. Sultan, 2008 (2) AWC 1337: 2008 (1) RD 398 (DB)

sections.title: 3. Settlement
sections.content: The settlement of land can be made in favour of persons referred to in sub-section (3) of Section 122-C if they have built their houses on any land held by tenure holder (not being Government lessees) and such house existed on 30th day of June, 1985. The restriction is only in respect of land held by Government lessee and such restriction is not applicable in respect of land held by tenure holders of other categories. In other words, if other conditions of Section 123(2) are satisfied, the land covered by house sites of persons enumerated under Section 122-C(3) shall be deemed to be settled with owners of such house by tenure holdpers of the land except upon the land of Government lessee.Ram Narain vs. Sub Divisional Officer, Kairana, 2008 (1) AWC 35 (DB)

sections.title: 4. SDO—Duty of
sections.content: Sub Divisional Officer was not authorised to settle the land without issuing notice to the Gaon Sabha/Land Management Committee. SDO also appears not to have given any reason, but simply approved the reports of Lekhpal and Kanoongo. This virtually amounts to dereliction of duty and delegation of power by S.D.O. to Lekhpal and Kanoongo which is not permissible. Ram Preet vs. Additional Commissioner, 2011 (5) AWC 5181

sections.title: 5. Nature of
sections.content: The provisions of Section 123(2) of the. Act, is prospective in nature and cannot be given a retrospective effect. Further, provisions of section 123 of the Act does not provide, either expressly or by necessary implication, to indicate, that from the appointed date, the valid decrees or orders of the Court would become void or would be rendered a nullity. These provisions do not give any overriding effect to any valid decree passed by a Court of law. In fact, the expression “notwithstanding anything contained in the Act” as given in section 123(2) is confined to the provisions of Zamindari Act, 1950. The said expression cannot be stretched to anything beyond Act. Majid vs. Rahmat Ullah, 2007 (102) RD 235

sections.title: 6. Benefit of Section 67A—Availability of
sections.content: There is nothing in Section 67-A of the Code which contemplates that such a right can only be claimed if the concerned party files a suit. The orders of Lower Court reflect that the petitioner was claiming protection of Section 67-A of the Code on the basis of certain materials. To expect such a person to get his rights adjudicated by way of a separate suit so as to claim the benefit of section 67-A would only promote multiplicity of proceedings which should be avoided. Suresh Chandra v. State of U.P. and others, 2018 (2) AWC 1675 (All)

sections.title: 68. Gaon Fund
sections.content:
(1) All sums received under this Code by a Gram Panchayat, Gram Panchayat or a Bhumi Prabandhak Samiti shall be credited to the Gaon Fund:
Provided that the amount of damages or compensation recovered under Section 67 shall be credited to the Consolidation Gaon Fund.
(2) The Gaon Fund constituted under the enactments repealed by this Code and subsisting immediately before the commencement of such Code shall be deemed to have been constituted under this section.
(3) The Gaon Fund shall be operated in such manner and shall be applied for such purposes as may be prescribed.

sections.title: 69. Consolidated Gaon Fund
sections.content:
(1) There shall be established for each district, a Consolidated Gaon Fund to which the following amounts shall be credited, namely : -
(a) the amount referred to in the proviso to sub-section (1) of Section 68;
(b) all contributions received by the Collector under sub-section (2);
(c) such other amounts as may be prescribed.
(2) Every Gram Panchayat in a district shall pay to the Collector annually such percentage, not exceeding twenty’ five, as the State Government may from time to time notify, of the total amount credited to the Gaon Fund under Section 67, in the manner prescribed.
(3) The Consolidated Gaon Fund shall be operated by the Collector and may be applied for the following purposes, namely : -
(a) the payment of fees and allowances, if any, of the lawyers appointed under Section 72;
(b) the payment of expenses incurred in connection with the conduct and prosecution of suits, applications or other proceedings by or against the Gram Panchayat or the Bhumi Prabandhak Samiti under this Code;
72[(c) the payment of expenses incurred on the development of lands of common utility, and
72 Substituted vide U.P. Act No. 7 of 2019 w.e.f. 10.03.2019. Earlier it read as under:
(c) such other amounts as may be prescribed.
(d) the payment of any other sum which the State Government may, by general or special order, declare to be an appropriate charge on such fund.
(4) The Consolidated Gaon Funds constituted under any of the enactments repealed by this Code and subsisting immediately before its commencement shall be deemed to have been constituted under this section.
73[(5) The State Government may, by notification in the Gazette, direct that a Consolidated Gaon Fund shall be established also for each tahsil for the purpose and in the manner prescribed.]
73 Inserted vide U.P. Act No. 4 of 2016 w.e.f. 16.12.2015

sections.title: 70. Orders and directions of the State Government and the Collector
sections.content:
(1) The State Government and, subject to its control, the Collector may issue such orders or directions to the Bhumi Prabandhak Samiti as may appear to be necessary for purposes of this Code.
(2) It shall be the duty of the Bhumi Prabandhak Samiti and its office bearers to forthwith carry out the orders and comply with the directions issued under sub-section (1).

sections.title: 1. Powers of SDM
sections.content: The power under Section 126 was delegated to Collector or S.D.M. who is also Assistant Collector first class in charge of a sub-division by Notification No. 6374-1-B-1 192-53 dated 8.3.1954. But the State Government or its delegate could exercise the power only for the reason mentioned in the section, namely, for purpose of the Act. The section is widely worded but the question is whether the order directing the L.M.C. to transfer Gaon Samaj land in favour of a private samiti can be considered to be a direction for purposes of the Act. The L.M.C. is constituted under Panchayat Raj Act but it is empowered under Section 122A of the Act with general superintendence, management, preservation and control of all land vested in the goon Sabha under Section 117 of the Act. It is one of the duties of L.M.C. under Section 122A (2) of the Act to settle and manage the land. Mathai Lal Dube vs. District Magistrate, 2000 (4) AWC 2752

sections.title: 2. Alternate remedy
sections.content: Against the order passed by SDM granting fishery lease in violation of the Government Order, an alternate remedy is available by filing an application before the Collector for cancelling the lease.Matsya Jeev Sahkari Samiti Ltd. vs. State, 2011 (1) UD 250 (UTT)

sections.title: 3. Issuance of Notification—competency of
sections.content: State Government is competent enough to issue necessary directions for maintenance and development of tanks, ponds and fisheries as well as settlement and management of lands. They are entitled to issue directions and instructions.Ram Kumar vs. State of U.P., 2001 RD 747

sections.title: 4. Fishery Lease
sections.content: Before passing an orders of allotment of the pond, SDM neither called any meeting of eligible person not any publicity was done, without such procedure followed, settlement held to be arbitrary and hence quashed. Matsya Jeev Sahkari Samiti Ltd. vs. State, 2011 (1) UD 250 (UTT). Where as in the case of Ram Kumar (2001 RD 747) it was held that it is not illegal that the settlement of fisheries has not been settled by holding public auction. see Prithvi Nathvs.State of U.P., 2002 RD 196

sections.title: 71. Alternative arrangement
sections.content:
If at any time the Collector is satisfied that -
(a) the Bhumi Prabandhak Samiti has failed without reasonable cause or excuse to discharge its duties or to perform the functions imposed or assigned to it by or under this Code; or
(b) circumstances have so arisen that the Bhumi Prabandhak Samiti is or may be rendered unable to discharge the duties or perform the functions imposed or assigned by or under this Code; or
(c) it is otherwise expedient or necessary to do so; he may, direct that the duties, powers and functions of such Bhumui Prabandhak Samiti under this Code, shall, notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, be discharged, exercised and performed by an officer not below the rank of a Naib-Tahsildar and for such period and subject to such restrictions as may be specified:
74[Provided that reasonable opportunity of hearing shall be given to the Bhumi Prabandhak Samiti before issuing any direction under this section.]

78 Substituted vide U.P. Act No. 4 of 2016 w.e.f. 16.12.2015
(2) The Collector may, on such terms and conditions and in such manner as may be prescribed, appoint not more than two Penal Lawyers (Revenue) for every tahsil.
(3) Subject to the provisions of sub-section (2) of Section 62, the legal practitioners appointed under sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) may plead or act, without any written authority, on behalf of any Gram Panchayat, Gram Panchayat or Bhumi Prabandhak Samiti in any Court or authority for which he is so appointed.
(4) No 79[Gram Sabha, Gram Panchayat or Bhumi Prabandhak Samiti], Panchayat or Bhumi Prabandhak Samiti shall engage any legal practitioner other than one appointed under this section without prior permission of the Collector.
79 Substituted vide U.P. Act No. 4 of 2016 w.e.f. 16.12.2015
(5) Notwithstanding anything contained in the Court Fees Act, 1870, (Act No. 7 of 1870) no Court fee shall be payable on any vakalatnama or memo of appearance filed by any legal practitioner appointed under this section.
(6) The legal practitioners appointed under this section shall not be competent to plead or act against any Gram Panchayat, Gram Panchayat or Bhumi Prabandhak Samiti before any Court for which he is so appointed.
80[(7) The State Government may, by notification in the Gazette, issue any difection, for monitoring of cases filed by or against Gram Panchayat, Gram Sabha or Bhumi Prabandhak Samiti and for performance based annual appraisal of Panel Advocates appointed under this Code or the enactments repealed by it, and also for appointing any law officer for the aforesaid purpose.]
80 Inserted vide U.P. Act No. 4 of 2016 w.e.f. 16.12.2015
**Scope of**
There is nothing that disentitles or disables a Gaon Sabha from contesting a case either as plaintiff or respondent by engaging counsel other than panel lawyer. Kishore vs. Gram Panchayat, 2013 (120) RD 319 (para 6)

sections.title: 73. Representation of Gram Panchayat
sections.content:
(1) In any suit or other proceedings under this Code, the Gram Panchayat shall be represented -
(a) in proceeding before the Collector or in a civil Court, by the District Government Counsel (Revenue);
(b) in proceeding before the Commissioner, by the Divisional Government Counsel (Revenue); and
(c) in proceeding before the Board or the High Court, by the separate Standing Counsels (Revenue) of Lucknow or Allahabad, as the case may be.
(2) Nothing in this Chapter shall preclude the State Government or the Collector from appointing special Counsel for the conduct of any suit or proceeding to which any Gram Panchayat is party on such terms and conditions as may be prescribed.
**Scope of—**
Provisions relating to land management, property and funds have now been statutorily also incorporated in the U.P. Revenue Code, 2006 read with U.P. Revenue Code Rules, 2016. A perusal of the said provisions would leave no room to doubt that the Gram Panchayat is to be represented by the Pradhan through an empanelled Lawyer and the Village Pradhan in a private capacity cannot pursue litigation on behalf of the Village Panchayat of the Gram Sabha in official capacity. Further, the petitioner in his own capacity individually could not have maintained such a petition but since the prayer made is in the larger interest of the villagers for grant of license for ensuring an effective public distribution system through the procedure prescribed under law, Court leave it open to the respondent No.4 to examine this and to take necessary steps in case the license has already not been granted for implementing the Government Order dated 17.8.2002 as well as the subsequent Government Orders in their true letter and spirit after following the due procedure prescribed therein within a reasonable time expeditiously. Vinod Kumar Mishra vs State of U.P., MISC. BENCH No. 14484 of 2016, decided on 23.6.2016 (DB) (per J. Amreshwar Pratap Sahi, Shamsher Bahadur Singh)

sections.title: 74. Classes of tenures
75. Bhumidhar with transferable rights
sections.content:
Every person belonging to any of the following classes, shall be called bhumidhar with transferable rights and shall have all the rights and be subject to all the liabilities conferred or imposed upon such bhumidhar by or under this Code, namely :-
(a) every person who was a bhumidhar with transferable rights immediately before the date of commencement of this Code.
(b) every person who in any other manner acquires, on or after the said date, the rights of such a bhumidhar under or in accordance with the provisions of this Code or under any other law for the time being in force.

sections.title: 76. Bhumidhar with non-transferable rights
sections.content:
(1) Every person belonging to any of the following classes shall be called a bhumidhar with non-transferable rights and shall have all the rights and be subject to all the liabilities conferred or imposed upon such bhumidhar by or under this Code, namely :-
(a) every person who was a bhumidhar with non-transferable rights immediately before the date of commencement of this Code;
(b) every person who is admitted as a bhumidhar with non-transferable rights on or after the said date by the Bhumi Prabandhak Samiti to any land under or in accordance with the provisions of this Code;
81[(c) every person who is allotted any land on or after the said date under the provisions of the Uttara Pradesh Bhoodan Yojna Act, 1952;
81 Substituted vide U.P. Act No. 4 of 2016 w.e.f. 16.12.2015. Earlier it read as under:
(c) every person who is or has been allotted any land under the provision of the Uttar Pradesh Bhodan Yajna Act, 1952;
(d) every person who is or has been allotted any land under the provision of the Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960
(d) every person who is allotted any land on or after the said date under the provisions of the Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960;]
82[(dd) every person who was an asami in possession of land not covered by Section 77 of this Code, immediately before the date of the commencement of this Code and had been recorded as such in Class 3 of the annual register (khatauni) of 1407 Fasli:
82 Inserted vide U.P. Act No. 4 of 2016 w.e.f. 16.12.2015
Provided that where the land in possession of a person, together with any other land, held by him in Uttar Pradesh exceeds the ceiling area determined under the Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, the rights of a Bhumidhar with non-transferable rights shall accrue in favour of such person in respect of so much area of the first mentioned land, as together with such other land held by him, does not exceed the ceiling area applicable to him, and the said area shall be demarcated in the prescribed manner in accordance with the principles laid down in the aforesaid Act;]
(e) every person who in any other manner acquires on or after the said date, the rights of such a bhumidhar under or in accordance with the provisions of this Code, or any other law for the time being in force.
(2) Every person who was a Bhumidhar with non-transferable rights immediately ‘before the commencement of this Code and had been such Bhumidhar for a period of 83[five years] or more shall become Bhumidhar with transferable rights on such commencement.
83 Substituted for “ten years” vide U.P. Act No. 4 of 2016 w.e.f. 16.12.2015
(3) Every person who was a Bhumidhar with non-transferable rights on the commencement referred to sub-sections (1) and (2) or becomes Bhumidhar with non-transferable rights after such commencement shall become Bhumidhar with transferable rights after expiry of five years from his becoming Bhumidhar with non-transferable rights.
(4) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other provisions of this Code, if any person transfers land by sale after becoming Bhumidhar with transferable rights 84[under sub-section (2) or sub-section (3)], he shall not be eligible for lease of any land vested in the Gram Panchayat or the State Government or the surplus land defined in the Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960.
84 Substituted “under sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) or sub-section (3)” vide U.P. Act No. 4 of 2016 w.e.f. 16.12.2015

sections.title: 3. Eviction
sections.content: Procedure

sections.title: 1. Scope of
sections.content: By virtue of the amendment made in this Section in the year 1969, the lease holders had become Sirdar on 1-7-1969 and as on the appointed day the plaintiff was in possession of the land in dispute and acquired rights as sirdar and by application of the provisions of Zamindari Act, he became Bhumidhar of the land. Thus on the date of alleged notification the plaintiff was bhumidhar of the land in suit and the alleged notification was issued in violation of the provisions made under the Indian Forest Act and was issued without jurisdiction. Thus the lower appellate Court was fully justified in holding that the plaintiff was the Bhumidhar and in possession over the land in suit and the landin suit is not a reserved forest. State of Uttaranchal vs. Lok Mani Sharma, AIR 2006 Utr 54

sections.title: 2. Effect of
sections.content: Held, petitioner becomes hereditary tenants of the disputed land on coming into the force of 1950 Act, he has become sirdar of the land hereunder, subsequently bhumidhar with transferable rights by operation of law. Gyan Singh vs. State of U.P., 2012 (1) UD 253

sections.title: 3. Eviction—Procedure
sections.content: Before any person is evicted from the land or property, servisng of notice regarding the same is mandatory. Mahndra vs. Additonal Commissioner, 2019 (2) ADJ 865

sections.title: 4. Object of
sections.content: Even the transfer by a Bhumidhar belonging to Scheduled Caste to a person belonging to Scheduled Caste shall be in accordance with the preference mentioned in sub-section (1). The object obviously is that transfer if made, the said transfer shall first go to landless agricultural labourer and thereafter to marginal farmer.Man Singh vs. Commissioner, Bareilly, 2008 (2) AWC 1998: 2008 (1) RD 598

sections.title: 5. Declaration of bhumidhari
sections.content: By virtue of Section 131-B, respondent’s father became bhumidhar with transferable rights on 14.1.1995, declaration to that effect declared on 4.3.2003, such orders are not in nature of grant of bhumidhari rights but only declaration to that effect hence the sale deed executed cannot be held to be null and void.Jaipal Singh vs. State of U.P., 2014 (114) RD 330 (para 5)

sections.title: 6. Benefit of
sections.content: Benefit of Section 131-B (2) could be extended only to those tenure holders to whom patta or lease were granted in accordance with law.Brihma Dutt Singh vs. Additional Commissioner, 2004 (1) RD 665 (Utt)

sections.title: 7. Suit for specific performance of agreement to sell
sections.content: The courts below found that the land in dispute was the Bhumidhari land with non-transferable rights of the defendants respondents, therefore, it was not liable to be transferred. Thus, it refused the decree of specific performance while exercising discretion under Section 20 of the Act. The land which cannot be transferred in law cannot be ordered to be transferred by the decree of the court. The courts below have therefore rightly refused to decree the suit for specific performance.Charan Singh vs. Dinesh Kumar, 2016 (2) AWC 1776

sections.title: 77. Bhumidhar rights not to accrue in certain lands
1. Garhi plot
sections.content: Section 132, makes it clear that notwithstanding anything contained in this Section, but without prejudice to Section 19, bhumidhari rights shall not accrue to any land covered by water. As plot in question is Garhi it cannot be part of consolidation scheme for allotment proceeding in the unit and as such it was rightly excluded by the DDC from the consolidation scheme. Under the Consolidation of Holdings Act ‘consolidation’ is defined under Section 3 (2)and Explanation (iii) of Section 3(2) of the Act makes it abundantly clear that land mentioned under Section 132 shall not be included in consolidation scheme. Iqbal Ahamad vs. DD C, 2005 (1) RD 580: 2005 (3) AWC 2423 (para 5&8)

sections.title: 2. Khalian
sections.content: Under Consolidation proceedings, land reserved for the purpose of khalian cannot be transferred by the Gaon Sabha to the petitioners.Dr. Ram Krishan Kanya Uchchatra Madhyamik Vidyalaya vs. State, 2009 (3) AWC 2510

sections.title: 3. Public utility land—Change of nature
sections.content: There is no provision hereunder to change nature of any public utility land and handing over that to a private person or body.Vishwanath Singh vs. Deputy Director, Consolidation, 2011 (4) AWC 4065

sections.title: 4. Determination of
sections.content: Any land, which is mentioned in section 132 of U.P.Z.A.&L.R. Act, can be allotted to any person, as defined in Section 198 sub section (1) with asami rights. The only area which requires determination is as to whether necessary safeguards have been followed or not. Mohammad Yamin vs. Additional Commissioner, 2012 (4) AWC

sections.title: 5. Whether declaration of right can be made in respect of public utilities land u/s. 132
sections.content: It is correct that the order dated 30.9.1983 refers to the land in question having been converted under an order dated 14th October, 1977 for the purpose of extending the benefit of a declaration in favour of the petitioner. Nonetheless there is no authority with the Sub Divisional Magistrate under the law for the time being in force to declare a land of public utility in the shape of a road/rasta as defined under Section 132 of the 1950 Act as an old parti. The record of settlement therefore could not have been altered by the Sub Divisional Magistrate under his executive order or even otherwise which has been made the basis of declaration in favour of the petitioner in the order dated 30.9.1983. Apart from this, the order dated 30.9.1983 also appears to have rested the enThe finding on the basis of such an entry in the Khatauni to give a declaration in favour of the petitioner. In the opinion of the Court the consequential action which is based on the order of 1977 also was equally erroneous and therefore in the opinion of the Court the Sub Divisional Magistrate did not commit any error in law to have set aside the order dated 30.9.1983 on 11.2.2009. Ram Adhar (Chamar) vs. Board of Revenue, U.P. at Allahabad, 2012 (2) AWC 1885

sections.title: 78. Asami
sections.content:
Every person belonging to any of the following classes, shall be called an asami, and shall have all the rights and be subject to all the liabilities conferred or imposed upon such asami by or under this Code, namely : -
89[(a) subject to the provisions of clause (dd) of sub-section (1) of Section 76 of this Code, every person who was an asami immediately before the date of commencement of this Code;]
89 Substituted vide U.P. Act No. 4 of 2016 w.e.f. 16.12.2015. Earlier it read as under:
(a) every person who was an asami immediately before the date of commencement of this Code;
(b) every person who is admitted as an asami on or after the said date by the Bhumi Prabandhak Samiti to any land under or in accordance with the provisions of this Code.
(c) every person who is admitted as lessee on or after the said date, by a bhumidhar of any land under or in accordance with the provisions of this Code;
(d) every person who in any other manner acquires the rights of an asami under or in accordance with the provisions of this Code or any other law for the time being in force.
**Asami–clasified**
So for as claim on the bais of long continuous possession is concerned, in view of Section 133(a) read with Section 202 of the Act, the right of the petitioners will remain as asami year to year through out and on the objection filed by respondent-2 they are liable for ejectment. Therefore, no better right can be conferred only on the basis of long continuous possesion. Naimuddin vs. A.D.M., (City)/ D.D.C., Gorakhpur 2015 (127) RD 183

sections.title: 79. Right of bhumidhars to exclusive possession
sections.content:
(1) A bhumidhar with transferable rights shall, subject to the provisions of this Code, have the right to exclusive possession of all laird of which he is such a bhumidhar and to use it for any purpose whatsoever.
(2) A bhumidhar with non-transferable rights shall, subject to the provisions of this Code, have the right to exclusive possession of all land of which he is such a bhumidhar, and to use such land for any purpose connected with agriculture.

90 Omitted vide UP Act No. 4 of 2021 w.e.f. 28.12.2020. Prior to omission it read as under:
80. Use of holding for Industrial, Commercial or Residential purpose.—(1) Where a bhumidhar with transferable rights uses his holding or part thereof, for industrial, commercial or residential purposes, the Sub-Divisional Officer may, suomotu or on an application moved by such bhumidhar, after making such enquiry as may be prescribed, either make a declaration that the land is being used for the purpose not connected with agriculture or reject the application. The Sub- Divisional officer shall take a decision on the application within forty five working days from the date of receipt of the application. In case the application is rejected, the Sub-Divisional officer shall state the reasons in writing for such rejection and inform the applicant of his decision.
Provided that if the application for declaration is accompanied with the prescribed fee and in case of joint holding, no objection of co-tenure holders is attached in case of co-tenure holder and if the declaration is not made by the Sub-Divisional Officer with forty-five days as aforesaid, then the declaration shall be deemed to have been made. Tehsildar will make a record of it in the revenue records, with the comment “subject to the order of the Sub-Divisional Officer”.
If any affected party wants to file an objection in relation to the said declaration, it may file an objection in the competent court. (This proviso was added by UP Act No.28 of 2020)
(2) Where a bhumidhar with transferable rights proposes to use in future his holding or part thereof, for industrial, commercial or residential purposes, the Sub- Divisional Officer may on an application moved by such bhumidhar, after making such enquiry as may be prescribed, either make a declaration that the land may be used for the purpose not connected with agriculture or reject the application, within forty five working days from the date of receipt of the application. In case the application is rejected, the Sub-Divisional officer shall state the reasons in writing of such rejection and inform the applicant of his decision:
Provided that for declaration under this sub-section there must exist a boundary wall surrounding the holding or part thereof, which is proposed to be used for such purpose:
Provided furher that if the bhumidhar fails to start the proposed non agricultural activity within a period of five years from the date of declaration under this sub-section, then the declaration under sub-section (2) for the holding or part thereof shall lapse:
Provided also that a declaration under this sub-section (2) shall not amount to change of land use and the land shall continue to be treated as agricultural land only. However, the bhumidhar shall be entitled to obtain loan and other necessary permissions, clearances etc. for the activity or project, proposed on the holding or part thereof, for which declaration under this sub-section has been obtained.
(3) A bhumidhar possessing declaration under sub-section (2) for his holding or part thereof, may apply to Sub-Divisional officer for converting declaration under sub-section (2) to a declaration under sub-section (1), after completion of construction activity or start of the proposed non- agricultural activity, within a period of five years from declaration under sub-section (2). On receipt of such an application, the Sub- Divisional officer, after making such enquiry as necessary, shall approve or reject the application within a period of 15 days from the receipt of the application. In case of rejection, he shall record in writing the reasons for such rejection:
Provided that for conversion of declaration under sub-section (2) to a declaration under sub-section (1), the bhumidhar shall be liable to pay only the balance amount of fee payable, calculated at prevailing circle rate, after adjusting the amount already paid by him for declaration under sub-section (2) earlier.
(4) No application for a declaration under sub-section (1) or (2), moved by any co-bhumidhar having undivided interest in bhumidhari land shall be maintainable, unless application is moved by all the co-bhumidhars of such bhumidhari land. In case only one of the co-bhumidhar wants to get a declaration for his share in the land with joint interest, then such an application shall be entertained only after the respective shares of the co-bhumidhars in the land have been divided in accordance with the provisions of law.
(5)The application for declaration under sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) shall contain such particulars and shall be made in such manner as may be prescribed.
(6)Where the application under sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) is made in respect of a part of the holding, the sub-divisional officer may, in the manner prescribed, demarcate such part for purposes of such declaration.
(7) No declaration under this section shall be made by the sub-divisional officer, if he is satisfied that the land or part thereof is being used or is proposed to be used for a purpose which is likely to cause a public nuisance or to affect adversely public order, public health, safety or convenience or which is against the uses proposed in the master plan.
(8) In case the land or part thereof for which a declaration under this section is being sought falls within the area notified under any Urban or Industrial Development Authority, then prior permission of the coyeemed Development Authority shall be mandatory.
(9) The State Government may fix the scale of fees for declaration under this section and different fees may be fixed for different purposs:
Provided that if the applicant uses the holding Air pat”hereof, for his own residential purpose, no fee shall be charged for the declaration under this section. (Substituted vide U.P. Act No. 7 of 2019 w.e.f. 10.03.2019)
Earlier was substituted vide U.P. Act No. 4 of 2016 w.e.f. 16.12.2015, it read as under:
80. Use of holding for Industrial, Commercial or Residential purpose.—(1) Where a Bhumidhar with transferable rights uses his holding or part thereof, for industrial, commercial or residential purposes, the Sub-Divisional Officer may, suo moth or on an application moved by such Bhumidhar, after making such enquiry as may be prescribed, either make a declaration that the land is being used for the purpose not connected with agriculture or reject the application. The Sub-Divisional Officer shall state the reasons in writing of such declaration or rejection and inform the applicant of this decision within forty-five working days from the date of receipt of the application:
(2) The application for declaration under sub-section (1) shall contain such particulars and shall be made in such manner as may be prescribed.
(3) Whore the application under sub-section (1) is made in respect of a part of the holding, the Sub-Divisional Officer may, in the manner prescribed, demarcate such part for purpose of such declaration.
(4) No declaration under this section shall be issued by the Sub-Divisional Officer, if he is satisfied that the land is to be used for a purpose which is likely to cause a public nuisance or to affect adversely public order, public health, safety or convenience or against uses proposed in the Master Plan.
(5) The State Government may fix the scale of fees for declaration under this section and different fees may be fixed for different purposes:
Provided that if the applicant uses the holding or part thereof for his own residential purpose, no fee shall be charged for the declaration under this section.
