Whenever proceedings are taken under this Chapter against any person for the recovery of any arrear of land revenue, he may pay the amount claimed to the recovery officer, and upon such payment the proceedings shall be stayed, and the person against whom such proceeding were taken may, notwithstanding anything contained in any other provisions of this Code, sue the State Government in the civil Court for the recovery of amount so paid.
**Scope of**
While exercising powers under Section 39 of U.P. Land Revenue Act, 1901, the Collector exercises the powers of an Executing Court and all questions going to root of liability, can be gone into as held by the Supreme Court in Seth Banarsi Das vs. District Magistrate1996 (2) SCC 689.Smt. Surinder Kaur vs. Collector, 1999 (1) AWC 773

sections.title: 204. Other payments not to be a valid discharge
sections.content: No payment on account of rent or other dues in respect of any land attached under this Chapter, made after such attachment, by the asami or any other person in possession thereof to any person other than the Revenue Officer authorised in this behalf shall operate as a valid discharge.

sections.title: 205. Applicability of the Chapter
sections.content: The provisions of this Chapter shall apply to the recovery of all arrears of land revenue and all other sums recoverable as an arrear of land revenue whether due before or after the commencement of this Code.

chapters.chapterTitle: Jurisdiction and Procedure of Revenue Courts

sections.title: 206. Jurisdiction of Civil Courts and Revenue Courts
sections.content:
(1) Notwithstan-ding anything contained in any law for the time being in force, but subject to the provisions of this Code, no Civil Court shall entertain any suit, application or proceeding to obtain a decision or order on any matter which the State Government, the Board, any revenue Court or revenue officer is, by or under this Code, empowered to determine, decide or dispose of.
(2) Without prejudice to the generality of the provisions of sub-section (1), and save as otherwise expressly provided by or under this Code -
(a) no civil Court shall exercise jurisdiction over any of the matters specified in the Second Schedule; and
(b) no Court other than the revenue Court or the revenue officer specified in 154[Column 3] of the Third Schedule shall entertain any suit, application or proceeding specified in 155[Column 2] thereof.
154 Substituted vide U.P. Act No. 4 of 2016 w.e.f. 16.12.2015
155 Substituted vide U.P. Act No. 4 of 2016 w.e.f. 16.12.2015
(3) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Code, an objection that a Court or officer mentioned in sub-section (2)(b) had or had no jurisdiction with respect to any suit, application or proceeding, shall not be entertained by any appellate, revisional or executing Court, unless the objection was taken before the Court or officer of the first instance, at the earliest opportunity, and in all cases where issues are settled at or before such settlement and unless there has been a consequent failure of justice.
**Scope of**
Per Section 206 of the Code, no Civil Court shall entertain any suit, application or proceeding to obtain a decision or order on any matter which the State Government, the Board, any Revenue Court or Revenue Officer is , by or under this Code, empowered to determine, decide or dispose of. Jahar Singh vs. State of U.P. , PIL No 32892 of 2016, decided on 31.01.2017, (per J. SP Kesarwani)

sections.title: 207. First appeal
sections.content:
(1) Any party aggrieved by a final ordenor decree passed in any suit, application or proceeding specified in 156[Column 3] of the Third Schedule, may prefer a first appeal to the Court or officer specified against it in 157[Column 4], where such order or decree was passed by a Court or officer specified against it in 158[Column 2] thereof
156 Substituted vide U.P. Act No. 4 of 2016 w.e.f. 16.12.2015
157 Substituted vide U.P. Act No. 4 of 2016 w.e.f. 16.12.2015
158 Substituted vide U.P. Act No. 4 of 2016 w.e.f. 16.12.2015
(2) A first appeal shall also lie against an order of the nature specified:
(a) in Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908; or
(b) in Section 104 of the said Code; or
(c) in Order XLIII Rule 1 of the First Schedule to the said Code.
(3) The period of limitation for filing a first appeal under this section shall be thirty days from the date of the order or decree appealed against.

sections.title: 208. Second Appeal
sections.content:
(1) Wherein any suit, application or proceeding specified in 159[Column 2] of the Third Schedule, any final order or decree is passed in any first appeal filed under Section 207, and any party to such appeal is aggrieved by it, such party may prefer a second appeal to the Court specified against it in 160[Column 5].
159 Substituted vide U.P. Act No. 4 of 2016 w.e.f. 16.12.2015
160 Substituted vide U.P. Act No. 4 of 2016 w.e.f. 16.12.2015
(2) The appellate Court shall not entertain a second appeal unless it is satisfied that the case involves a substantial question of law.
(3) The period of limitation for filing a second appeal under this section shall be ninety days from the date of the order or decree appeal against.

sections.title: 1. Scope of
sections.content:
Sections 209 and 331 of Act, when read together, shows that suit, had to be filed in a Special Court created under the Act within a period of limitation specially prescribed under the Rules made under the Act, and the jurisdiction of the ordinary Civil Courts to entertain the suit was absolutely barred. Since the Civil Court which entertained the suit suffered from an inherent lack of jurisdiction because of special provisions of the Act, 1951, the present appeal filed by the appellants had to be dismissed.Deokinandan vs. Surajpal, 1995 SCC, Supl. (4) 671: JT 1995 (8) 150: 1996 RD 70 see also Shankar vs. Surendra Singh Rawat, AIR 2007 Utt 15
The term ‘shall not’ followed by the term ‘unless’ itself reflects restrictive nature of Section 208 of the U.P. Revenue Code, 2006 and the language of the same is indicative of the legislative intention that the legislature did not want Second Appeal to become a ‘third trial on facts’. It would not be out of place to mention here that the term ‘shall not’ in its ordinary significance is a mandatory prohibition and the courts should ordinarily give that interpretation to that term unless such an interpretation leads to some absurd or inconvenient consequence or be it variance with the intent of the legislature, to be collected from other parts of the Act. It is a settled principle of rule of interpretation that whenever a statute requires a particular act to be done in a particular manner, then such act has to be done in that manner only and in no other manner. Awadhesh Singh vs. State of Uttar Pradesh, 2023:AHC:193842
For the party who seeks to oust the jurisdiction of civil court to establish his contention and that a statute ousting the jurisdiction of a civil court must be strictly construed. Abdul Waheed Khan vs. Bhawani and others, 1968 RD 79: AIR 1966 SC 1718.

sections.title: 2. Non-framing of substantial question of law by second appellate Court—effect of
sections.content:
The reversal of the final order and decree passed in appeal by the court below in exercise of its jurisdiction under Section 208 of the U.P. Revenue Code, 2006 is impermissible without formulating substantial question of law and a decision on such question, however, in the event of concurrence with the court below the formulation of substantial question of law is not a sine qua non and the same will not render the judgment of the second appellate court vitiated. Awadhesh Singh vs. State of UP and others, 2023 (12) ADJ 554
The concurrent findings of fact are to be considered as settled facts of the case and the High Court should ordinarily restrain itself from interfering with the concurrent findings of fact. The said restrain is on a much higher footing in cases where the High Court is not the appellate Court, rather, it is exercising its Writ jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. refer Gurvachan Kaur and others vs. Salikram (Dead) through LRS, (2010) 15 SCC 530 and Santosh Hazari vs. Purushottam Tiwari (Deceased) by LRS. (2001) 3 SCC 179

sections.title: 3. “Cause of action” —pivotal point for determining jurisdiction
sections.content: Section 331 of the Act makes the phrase ‘’cause of action’’ as pivotal point for determining the jurisdiction of civil or revenue court. The expression ‘’cause of action’’ means every fact that would be necessary for the plaintiff to prove in order to support his right of judgment. It is the real ‘’cause of action’’ which determines the jurisdiction of the court to entertain particular action notwithstanding the language used in the plaint or the relief claimed. The strength on which the plaintiff comes to the court does not depend upon the defence or relief claimed which could determine the forum for the entertainment of claim and grant of relief. It is the pith and substance which is to be seen. The expression ‘’any relief’’ used in Section 331 of the Act is of too wide import and would not only mean the relief claimed but would also include any relief arising out of the cause of action which led the plaintiff to invoke the jurisdiction of a court of law. The word ‘relief’ is not part of cause of action nor the same is related to the defence set up in the case. The relief is a remedy which the court grants from the facts asserted and proved in an action. Mangoo Singh and ors. vs. Ram Autar, 2024:AHC:133948

sections.title: 4. Plea to bar of jurisdiction —consideration under
sections.content:
A plea of bar to jurisdiction of a civil court must be considered having regard to the contentions raised in the plaint. For the said purpose, averments disclosing cause of action and the reliefs sought for therein must be considered in their enThety. The court may not be justified in determining the question, one way or the other, only having regard to the reliefs claimed dehors the factual averments made in the plaint. With a view to determine the question as regards exclusion of jurisdiction of the civil court in terms of the provisions of the Act, the court has to consider what, in substance, and not merely in form, is the nature of the claim made in the suit and the underlying object in seeking the real relief therein. Church of North India vs. Lavajibhai Ratanjibhai, (2005) 10 SCC 760
This case before the Supreme Court had arisen out of a suit for cancellation of sale deed dated 15.06.2006 in respect of an agricultural land filed before the Civil Court. A question arose before the Apex Court whether the decision of the District Court and High Court holding the civil suit as maintainable despite bar of Section 331 of the Act of 1950 was correct. The Supreme Court, after discussing the judgments of Ram Padarath161 (supra), Shri Ram162 and Kamla Prasad163, held that the suit before the Civil Court was very much maintainable. Narendra Kumar Mittal and others vs. Nupur Housing Development Pvt. Ltd. and another, 2019 (7) Supreme 157: 2019 (144) RD 785 (SC)
161 1989 RD 21 (FB)(All)
162 (2001) 3 SCC 24
163 (2007) 4 SCC 213

sections.title: 5. Registered instrument is not cancelled—effect of
sections.content: So long as a registered instrument is not cancelled by civil court, revenue court will be bound to respect it and will not able to ignore it, as held by Full Bench of Allahabad Court in Ram Nath vs. Munna, 1976 RD 220 (FB).

sections.title: 6. Cancellation of Will
sections.content: The suit for cancellation of the Will was very much maintainable before the Civil Court. Mangoo Singh and ors. vs. Ram Autar, 2024:AHC:133948

sections.title: 7. Mutation neither creates nor extinguishes title
sections.content: The mutation in revenue records neither creates nor extinguishes title of the person and such entries are relevant only for the purpose of collecting land revenue. As such, the court of competent jurisdiction while deciding the title over the property must not be influenced by any finding or observation made in the mutation orders or during mutation proceedings. Amritansh Pandey versus State of U.P. and others; reported in 2023 (161) RD 178

sections.title: 8. Applicability of
sections.content: For application of the provisions of Section 331 of the 1950 Act which has been incorporated in the 1956 Act, it was necessary for the defendants to prove that the suit lands had been demarcated by the State Government. Unless the land is vested in the State Government, the provisions of Section 331 of the 1950 Act would have no application to oust the jurisdiction of the Civil Court. Mahant Dooj Das vs. Udasin Panchayati Bara Akhara, 2008 (3) AWC 2569: 2008 (2) RD 719 (SC): 2008 (6) JT 267 (para 18)

sections.title: 9. Ejectment of Asamis
sections.content: Dismissing the appeal, apex court held that, the only ground on which the suit was held to be barred was that the appellants were asamis and their ejectment could not be granted by the Civil Court. Kali Prasad vs. Deputy Director of Consolidation, 2000 RD 549

sections.title: 10. Question of Law
sections.content: The appeal before Board of Revenue would lie on a question of law. State of Uttarakhand (Prevs.U.P.) vs. Mohan Singh, CIVIL APPEAL NO. 6479. of 2012 decided on 12 September, 2012 (para 27)

sections.title: 11. Substantial question of law
sections.content:
Since the High Court has omitted to frame substantial questions of law and answer the same and thus has failed to discharge its duty under S. 100 of the CPC hence the judgment and decree of the High Court be set aside. Amar Nath vs. Kewla Devi, (2014) 11 SCC 273. Reffered & relied on Surat Singh vs. Hukam Singh Negi ((2010) 15 SCC 525) and Hardeep Kaur vs. Malkiat Kaur ((2012) 4 SCC 344).
The right of appeal to the Board of Revenue under sub-section (4) of Section 331 clearly intended to be limited to the grounds set out in the then existing Section 100, since those were the grounds which were before the Legislature and to which the Legislature could have applied its mind and it is reasonable to assume that it was with reference to those specific and known grounds that the Legislature intended to limit the right of appeal. The appeal before the Board of Revenue would, therefore, lie on a question of law. State of Uttarakhand (previously State of Uttar Pradesh) vs. Mohan Singh (SC)

sections.title: 12. Jurisdiction of
sections.content:
Where in a suit, from a perusal only of the reliefs claimed, one or more of them are ostensibly cognizable only by civil court and at least one relief is cognizable only by the revenue court, further questions which arise are whether all the reliefs are based on the same cause of action and, if so, (a) whether the main relief asked for on basis of that cause of action is such as can be granted only by a revenue court, or (b) whether any real or substantial relief (though it may not be identical with that claimed by the plaintiff) could be granted by the revenue court. There can be no doubt that in all cases contemplated under (a) and (b) above the jurisdiction shall vest in the revenue court and not in the civil court. In all other cases of a civil nature the jurisdiction must vest in civil court. Ram Awalamb vs. Jata Shankar, AIR 1969 All 526 (FB)
Jurisdiction of civil court barred for trying suits for cancellation of sale deed filed by a person whose name is not recorded in revenue records. Jai Singh vs. IInd ADJ, Muzaffarnagar, 2001 RD 817: 2001 (4) AWC 2826: 2001 (4) ALR 580.Where a recorded tenure holder, having prima facie title and is in possession of land files suit for cancellation of sale deed having obtained it fraudulently or by impersonation, Revenue Courts not a proper forum. Shri Ram vs. Ist ADJ, 2001 RD 241: 2001 (1) AWC 862 (SC): (2001) 3 SCC 24
(1973) 2 SCC 535 distinguished. 1989 RD 21 and (1990) 1 SCC 207 referred to.Revenue courts are neither equipped nor competent to effectively adjudicate on allegations of fraud that has overtones of criminality and courts really skilled and experienced to try such issues are courts constituted under Code of Civil Procedure. Horil vs. Keshav, (2012) 5 SCC 525
A finding recorded by civil court on question of jurisdictional fact is binding on parties to suit. Kali Prasad vs. Deputy Director of Consolidation, 2000 RD 549

sections.title: 13. Burden of Proof
sections.content: The ouster of jurisdiction of a civil court is not readily accepted and heavy burden of proof lies on the party who asserts that the civil court’s jurisdiction is ousted and some other court, tribunal or authority has been vested with jurisdiction. Mahant Dooj Das vs. Udasin Panchayati Bara Akhara, 2008 (3) AWC 2569: 2008 (2) RD 719 (SC) (para 17)

sections.title: 14. Agricultural Land
sections.content:
Appellants contention that Revenue Court has jurisdiction in respect of the controversy as to the use of the land whether it is an agricultural land or not? Held ‘No’. Chandrika Singh vs. Raja Vishwanath Pratap Singh, 1992 AIR 1318: (1992) 3 SCC 90 (para 9) held not applicable in Kulwant Kaur Sidhu vs. Smt. Rahiman Bai Guddi, 2006 (100) RD 626: 2006 (2) AWC 1806 (Utt.).
The jurisdiction of a Civil Court is barred in respect of agricultural land. Madan Mohan Mishra vs. Chandrika Pandey, (2009) 3 SCC 720 see also Amar Nath vs. Kewla Devi (SC) on 22 April, 2014 see also Bhim Bahadur vs. Vikram Singh, 2016 (1) UAD 391
Suit for claim of relief of injunction in respect of agricultural land by tenure holder is not barred by Section 333 of the Act.Kulwant Kaur Sidhu vs. Rahiman Bai Guddi Guddi Chaudhary, 2006 (100) RD 626 (Utt HC)
Suit for declaration claiming a sale deed void and nullity being fraudulently executed by someone else other than by plaintiff being actual owner, the suit was not maintainable in civil court and could be filed in a revenue court is correct.Babu Nandan (D) vs. Smt. Esraji, 2003 (4) AWC 2972 relied on Azahar Hasan vs. District Judge, 1998 (3) AWC 2024 (SC): JT 1998 (4) SC 313

sections.title: 15. Abadi land
sections.content: The disputed land being an Abadi land and it is not being used as the agricultural land hence suits not barred by the provisions of Section 331 of the Act.State of U.P. vs. R.B. Narain Singh Sugar Mills Ltd., AIR 2007 Utr 87: 2007 UAD 725 (DB)

sections.title: 16. Fraud and impersonation
sections.content:
Held, where a recorded tenure-holder having a prima facie title and in possession filed suit in the civil court for cancellation of sale deed having been obtained on the ground of fraud or impersonation cannot be directed to file a suit for declaration, in the Revenue Court, the reason being that in such a case, prima facie, the title of the recorded tenure-holder is not under cloud. He does not require declaration of his title to the land. The position would be different where a person not being a recorded tenure-hold and seeks cancellation of sale deed by filing a suit in the civil court on ground of fraud or impersonation. There necessarily plaintiff is required to seek declaration of his title and therefore, may be directed to approach Revenue Count, as sale deed being, void has to be ignored for giving hint relief for declaration/possession.Shri Ram vs. Ist Additional District Judge, 2001 RD 241:(2001) 3 SCC 24 (para 15)
The Supreme Court Horil vs. Keshav, (2012) 5 SCC 525in has expanded the scope in case of the jurisdiction of the Civil Court to decide the issue of fraud and has held that the Civil Courts can entertain suit even in regard to decrees or orders passed in suit or proceedings under different statute or tribunal of limited jurisdiction.
Prayer for quashing of order obtained by fraud can be challenged in civil court. The suit was not barred under the aforesaid provisions as the UP Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act has no jurisdiction to deal with the subject matter. Amar Nath vs. Kewla Devi on 22 April, 2014

sections.title: 17. Question of Jurisdiction—conditions for
sections.content:
It is settled by a catena of decisions that the question as to bar of civil courts’ jurisdiction cannot be resolved merely by having a look at the relief claimed. A question of jurisdiction can be raised only if the conditions are satisfied, which are namely, (a) the objection to the jurisdiction must have been taken in the Court of first instance and in all cases where issues are settled, at or before such settlement and (b) the consequence of entertaining suit by the civil court has been a failure of justice. Smt. Mangli Devi vs. Kamlesh Kumar, 2004 (2) AWC 1274 (para 8)
The conditions that must be satisfied before the question of jurisdiction can be raised before an appellate or revisional court. Firstly, the objection must be taken before the trial court at the earliest stage and secondly, the party must show that there has been failure of justice on account of the suit being tried by the Civil Court. if either of the two conditions are not fulfilled it is not open to party to raise the question of Jurisdiction before appellate Court or the revisional Court and a decree or order passed by the Civil Court shall be valid notwithstanding the provisions contained in Section 331 of the Act. Sabha Chand vs. Narayan Singh, 1981 ALR 298 (DB),
Provisions of Section 331(1-A) debars a litigant from raising the question of jurisdiction either of the civil or of the revenue court in an appeal of revisional court unless the two conditions mentioned in it are satisfied.Thakur Dhyan Singh vs. Indra Pal Singh, 1973 ALJ 193:AIR 1973 All 243
Objection relating to jurisdiction under Section 331 of the Act is to be raised at the earliest but by the exercise of jurisdiction by the Courts (other than mentioned in Column 4 of Schedule II)failure of justice should have resulted.Satyendra @ Babu vs. Smt. Phullan, 2013 (1) UD 500 (UTT)

sections.title: 18. Expression ‘any relief’
sections.content: The introduction of the expression ‘any relief’ in Section 331 of the Act in place of the expression used earlier, namely, “adequate relief” was not really intended to imply that the relief which the revenue court can grant, need not be a relief adequate to the relief claimed in the civil court. A relief which fails to relieve cannot be a relief at all, the relief which the revenue court should be in a position to grant must be a real relief to the plaintiff. Ram Awalamb vs. Jata Shankar, 1968 RD 470: AIR 1969 All 526 (FB) (para 102)

sections.title: 19. Cognizance of suits
sections.content: Section 331 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act excludes the jurisdiction of civil court in respect of those matters which relief can be had from the revenue court by means of a suit, application or proceedings mentioned in Schedule II to the ‘Act’. Section 331 of the Act, if read without Explanation, does not create any difficulty. Ram Padarath vs. IInd ADJ, 1989 (15) ALR 19 (FB)

sections.title: 20. Applicability of
sections.content:
Suit for cancellation of a sale deed or other instruments and documents are essentially suits of civil nature. Every suit of civil nature is cognizable by a civil court except cognizance of which is expressly or impliedly barred.Ram Padarath vs. IInd ADJ, 1989 (15) ALR 19 (FB) see also Ram Kunwar Singh vs. Pramod Kumar, 2007 (4) AWC 3414
Where the plaintiff is not a recorded tenure holder and seeks relief of injunction, it can be said that he is seeking declaration of title but where he is a recorded tenure holder, it cannot be said that the suit is not within the jurisdiction of civil court for granting relief of injunction in respect of agricultural land. Ram Avalambh vs. Jatashanker & Ors, 1968 RD 470 (FB)
Where the recorded tenure holder files the suit for injunction, Civil Court has jurisdiction to try the suit. Kamla Prasad vs Sri Krishna Kant Pathak, 2007 AIR SCW 1403: (2007) 4 SCC 213: 2007 (3) ALJ 165: AIR 2007 SC (Supp) 618: (2007) 102 RD 378: (2007) 2 AWC 1764
Normally, Section 331 of the U.P. Z.A. & L.R. Act is attracted in such cases where a declaration of right or status of a tenure holder is necessarily needed. A recorded tenure holder or a person having possession over the land in question being Bhumidhar cannot be denied the relief by civil court on the ground of nonmaintainability of suit in view of Section 331 of the U.P. Z.A. & L.R. Act. Brij Kishore v. Rajesh Kumar Gupta, 2018 (5) ALJ 331

sections.title: 21. Suit under Section 176
sections.content: A reference to Schedule II would show that the court of original jurisdiction for a suit under Section 176 of the Act for division of a holding of a Bhumidhar is Assistant Collector, First Class and the courts of First Appeal and Second Appeal are Commissioner and the Board of revenue respectively. Horil vs. Keshav, (2012) 5 SCC 525

sections.title: 22. Schedule II
sections.content: Section 331 read with Schedule II bars jurisdiction of civil court only in respect of such reliefs which are mentioned in Schedule II and for their adjudication another authority has been prescribed thereunder. The only ground on which the suit was held to be barred was that the appellants were asamis and their ejectment could not be granted by the civil court. A finding recorded by the civil court on the question of jurisdictional fact is binding on the parties to the suit. Kali Prasad vs. DDC, AIR 2000 SC 3722

sections.title: 23. Revenue Records
sections.content: Suit for cancellation of sale deed by persons not recorded in Revenue RecordsJai Singh vs. IInd ADJ, 2001 RD 817: 2001 (4) AWC 2826: 2001 (4) ALR 580 or not party to suit Sumer Chand vs. Divisional Commissioner, 2003 (1) RD 569 (Utt), is maintainable by Civil Court.

sections.title: 24. Rights over the Sir land
sections.content: When documents not executed by the plaintiff vendor and moreover the plaintiff born before the enforcement of the Zamindari Abolition Act, he has rights over the Sir land and hence the suit for cancellation filed in Civil Court just and proper. Kalindi vs. IIIrd ADJ, 2001 RD 546: 2001 (3) AWC 1978: 2001 (4) ALR 265

sections.title: 25. Will
sections.content: In the case of Azhar Hussain vs. District Judge Saharanpur, 1998 (89) RD 493 (SC), the Apex Court held that the question as to who should be recorded as a tenant is determinable by the revenue authorities. Whereas Allahabad High Court in Deokinandan (Deokinandan vs. Suraj Pal, 1996 RD (87)), held that jurisdiction of civil court for deciding a dispute of title to land is barred because the land is covered by provisions of U.P.Z.A. and L.R. Act. Where plaintiff was already recorded in the revenue record having prima facie title and he was not a third party which may necessitate to seek declaration of his right or title over the land in revenue courts and in case the decision of the civil court leans in favour of cancellation of the Will, his name would come to be restored automatically by ministerial act of the revenue authorities.Radhey Shyam vs. Raj Kishore, 2004 (4) AWC 3656

sections.title: 26. Declaration of title
sections.content: Suit for declaration of title could be maintained only in Revenue Courts.Devendra Mehta vs. Nathu Singh, 2009 (2) UD 528 (UTT)

sections.title: 27. Re-assesment of evidence
sections.content: Board of Revenue cannot reassess evidence of the parties in Second Appeal.Keshav Chand vs. Board of Revenue, 2008 (2) UD 340

sections.title: 28. Suit for Possession
sections.content:
Suit for possession and other rights over agricultural land not entertainable by Civil Courts.Chandrika Misir vs. Bhaiya Lal, (1973) 2 SCC 474, see also Deoki Nandan vs. Surajpal, JT 1995 (8) 150
Civil Court had jurisdiction to grant relief of possession in respect of land which is pleaded to have been settled to him under Section 9.Mussadi vs. Mangal, 2009 (2) UD 557

sections.title: 29. Injunction
sections.content:
Jurisdiction vests with Revenue Court. Arvind Singh Bisht vs. IInd ADJ, Nainital, 2004 (2) RD 493 (Utt) see also Sandeep Kumar vs. Additional Civil Judge, 2005 (1) RD 756
Where the plaintiff is not a recorded tenure holder who seeks injunction and thereby under the garb of that desires to get declared title holder from Civil Court, such a suit not maintainable before the Civil Court. Milikat Singh vs. Bhajan Singh, 2008 (1) UD 669 see also 2006 (1) UD 650
If the name is not recorded in revenue records, injunction suit pertaining to agricultural land is not maintainable in Civil Court, Mohd Aslam vs. Harendra Singh Negi, 2014 (1) UD 187, whereas simpliciter injunction suit is maintainable in Civil Court.Hemlata Walia vs. Civil Judge (Jr. Division), 2007 (2) UD 632 (UTT)

sections.title: 30. Mense profit
sections.content: The instant is a suit for recovery of mesne profits. This suit accordingly is not covered by the provisions of Section 209. A partition is not necessary for recovery of mesne profits. Mohammad Abdul Jalil Khan vs. Mohammad Abdul Salam Khan, AIR 1933 All 519. The suit accordingly does not fall under any of the items mentioned in column III of Schedule II of the Zamindari Abolition Act. It was accordingly rightly held to be cognizable by the Civil Court.Durg Pal Singh vs. Pratap Singh, 1982 RD 289

sections.title: 31. Void and Voidable suits
sections.content:
Since thefraudulent misrepresentation was with respect to the contents and not the character of the document the transaction was not void but only voidable. Ningawwa vs. B.S. Hireknrabnar, AIR 1968 SC 956. A voidable document is one which remains in force until set aside and such a document can be set aside only by a competent civil court. A suit for that purpose would, therefore, be maintainable. A claim that a transaction is void is, however, a matter which can be adjudicated upon by the consolidation authorities. Smt. Dularia Devi vs. Janardan Singh, 1990 AIR 1173: 1990 SCC (Supp) 216
Supreme Court inBismillah vs. Janeshwar Prasad, AIR 1990 SC 540, held suit for cancellation of void and voidable sale deed shall lie in civil court. If there was fraudulent misrepresentation in respect of character of a document, then document would be void and consolidation authorities have jurisdiction to ignore it. Smt. Dularia Devi vs. Janardan Singh, AIR 1990 SC 1173
In a suit instituted before a civil court for cancellation of an instrument, with respect to an agricultural land, if a plea with respect to the bar of section 331 of the UP ZA & LR Act is take1n, the court must first determine as to whether from the plaint averments the instrument, as alleged, is void or voidable. If the plaint averments go to show that the instrument is voidable at the instance of the plaintiff(s), then the suit would be maintainable in a civil court, but if it is alleged to be void then the Court may have to undertake a complex exercise so as to assess whether in a given set of facts a declaration of right or status of a tenure holder is necessarily needed or not. If a declaration to that effect is necessarily needed, in that event, the relief for cancellation would be mere surplusage and redundant, because the court, which has power to grant declaration can disregard a void document while granting a declaratory relief. In such an event a civil suit would be barred by sub section (1) of Section 331 of the UP ZA & LR Act. As the revenue court has no power to pass a decree of cancellation of a document, the suit would lie before the Civil Court irrespective of the fact that name of the defendant-appellants have been entered in the revenue record consequent to the execution of the sale-deed. Ganga Prasad vs. Ram Das, 2014 (4) ALJ 492 (All)
O. XLIII R.1 of CPC referred to in S. 331(4) of UPZA & LR Act, 1950 and in S. 207 of UP Revenue Code, 2006 provides for a list of orders against which an appeal is maintainable. Remedy of appeal is not available against an order rejecting an application under Order VII, Rule 11 of CPC or an order declining to dispose of an application under Order VII, Rule 11 of CPC. Thus, such an order is not appealable. Therefore, an order rejecting an application under Order VII, Rule ll of CPC or an order declining to dispose of an application under Order VII, Rule 11 of CPC, would be revisable. Sushil Kumar v. Addl. Commissioner Judicial-I, Lucknow and ors., 2024(3) ADJ 76 (LB)
When the defendants obtained thumb impression of the plaintiff on the sale deed by telling her that the documents on which she was affixing her thumb impression related to grant of old age pension and that she was not given any amount as sale consideration and that plaintiff was in possession. Suit or action for cancellation of void document will generally lie in the Civil Court and a party cannot be deprived of his right getting this relief permissible under law except when a declaration of right or status and a tenure-holder is necessarily needed in which event relief for cancellation will be surplusage and redundant. A recorded tenure-holder having prima facie title in his favour can hardly be directed to approach the Revenue Court in respect of seeking relief for cancellation of a void document which made him to approach the Court of law and in such case he can also claim ancillary relief even though the same can be granted by the Revenue Court. Anju vs. Vikram Kaur, 2013 (119) RD 564 (All)
If a plaintiff comes to the civil court for seeking cancellation of deed which may be void or voidable, whether the name of the plaintiff is recorded or not, the Jurisdiction of the civil court not having been expressly barred to try such suits, the suit will be maintainable in the civil court.Shri Narain Mishra vs. IV Addl. District Judge, 2004(96) RD 273: 2001 (4) AWC 2826 see also Jai Singh vs. 2nd ADJ, 2001 ALJ 2621 (All), Dr. Ayodhya Prasad vs. Gangotri, 1981 ALJ 647, Gorakh Nath Dube vs. Hari Narain Singh, 1973 RD 423, Indra Deo vs. Smt. Ram Pyari, 1982 ALJ 1308, Ram Padarath vs. IInd Additional District Judge, 1981 AWC 1 (FB), Smt. Bismilla vs. Janeshwar Prasad, 1990 (1) AWC 359 (SC) : AIR 1990 SC 540, Smt. Sumitra Devi vs. ADJ, 2000 RD 45, Smt. Rasheedan vs. Amar Singh, 1998 (16) LCD 177, Mahabir Singh vs. District Judge, Fatehpur, 1998 (89) RD 540, Smt. Chhanga vs. 1st ADJ, Jaunpur, 1998 (89) R.D. 647

sections.title: 32. Insertion of names—Record of Rights
sections.content: Courts below were right in coming to the conclusion that legality or otherwise of insertion of names of purchasers in Record of Rights and deletion of name of the plaintiff from such record can only be decided by Revenue Court since the names of the purchasers had already been entered into. Only Revenue Court can record a finding whether such an action was in accordance with law or not and it cannot be decided by a Civil Court.Kamla Prasad vs. Sri Krishna Kant Pathak, 2007 (4) SCC 213: 2007 (102) RD 378.

sections.title: 33. Decree by minor
sections.content: The Apex Court held that the judgment or decree can be avoided by the minor in the later proceeding on the ground of gross negligence or fraud or collusion.Asharfilal vs. Koili, AIR 1995 SC 1440: (1995) 4 SCC 163 (3 Judges)

sections.title: 34. Aplication of Limitation Act—Void transaction
sections.content: If the plaintiff is in possession of a property, he may file a suit for declaration that the deed is not binding upon him but if he is not in possession thereof, even under a void transaction, the right by way of adverse possession may be claimed. Thus, it is not correct to contend that the provisions of the Limitation Act would have no application at all in the event the transaction is held to be void.Prem Singh vs. Birbal, 2006 (101 RD 260 (SC): 2006 (5) SCC 353

sections.title: 35. Jurisdiction—Tests for determination—civil or revenue court
sections.content: If the court is competent to grant the main relief asked for in the plaint then the ancillary relief can also be granted by that court. The twin tests for determination of the jurisdiction of civil or revenue courts depend upon: (a) Cause of action (b) Main relief. Ram Mangal vs. Bindhyachal, 1964 ALJ 1026 see also Mohd. Khalil Khan vs. Mahbub Ali, AIR 1949 P.C. 78, Indra Deo vs. Smt. Ram Pyari, 1982 ALJ 1308, Ram Awalamb vs. Jata Shanker, 1968 RD 470 (All)(FB)

sections.title: 36. Trespasser—Suit against
sections.content: It was held by a Division Bench of Allahabad, that a suit for demolition and possession against a trespasser may lie in a civil court.Angnu vs. Mahabir, 1954 All LJ 669

sections.title: 37. Test of main & ancillary relief to determine jurisdiction
sections.content: Held that, (a) the main relief is cognizable by a revenue court the suit would be cognizable by the revenue court only. The fact that the ancillary reliefs claimed are cognizable by civil court would be immaterial for determining the proper forum for the suit; (b) the main relief is cognizable by the civil court the suit would be cognizable by the civil court only and the ancillary reliefs, which could be granted by the revenue court may also be granted by the civil court. Allahabad High Court further held that, above principle will apply also to a suit for injunction and demolition relating to agricultural land and brought against a trespasser.Ram Awalamb vs. Jata Shanker, 1968 RD 470 (All)(FB): AIR 1969 All 526 see also Chhedi vs. Smt. Indrapati, AIR 1972 All 446

sections.title: 38. Counter claim to evidence
sections.content: Held, if a counter claim is permitted to be set up after the evidence is adduced, it would cause great prejudice to the plaintiff in the suit, because he would not be aware of adducing evidence against the counter claim. The framers of the law never intended the pleading by way of counter claim being utilized as an instrument for forcing upon a reopening of the trial or pushing back the progress of proceeding. In no case, the counter claim is not entertainable when the trial had already commenced.Dr. T.D. Padalia and another vs. District Judge, AIR 2008 Utt 11, see also Ramesh Chand vs. Anil Panjwani, (2003) 7 SCC 350, Saleem Bhai vs. State of Maharashtra, AIR 2003 SC 759, Smt. Sumitra Devi vs. Ist ADJ, Basti, 1999 (90) RD 658 (All), Ashok Kumar Srivastav vs. National Insurance Company Ltd., (1998) 4 SCC 361, M/s Bharat Petroleum Corp. Ltd vs. Smt. Parvati Devi, 1998 (32) ALR 149, T. Arvindandam vs. Satyapal, AIR 1977 SC 2421

sections.title: 39. Evidence when can be taken to decide jurisdiction
sections.content: The controversy in the present suit is as to on which date the petitioner’s father had expired and whether the sale deed was executed by petitioner’s father during his life time or was executed by an imposter after the death of the petitioner’s father. This question can only be decided on the basis of the evidence adduced by the civil court.Smt. Sharda Devi vs. ADJ (Special Judge), Gorakhpur, 1998 (89) RD 278 (All): 1998 (2) AWC 919 see also Ganga vs. Buddhi Ram, 1965 RD 300 (All)

sections.title: 40. Stage of raising plea of want of jurisdiction
sections.content:
In the year 1969, Sec. 331 of the UPZA & LR Act 1950 was amended by adding sub section (1-A) to it with the result that if the plea of want of jurisdiction was not raised before the trial court, the same cannot be raised in appeal, revision or in execution proceedings. Even if the plea of want of jurisdiction was taken in the trial court, the same can not be raised before the appellate or revisional court unless there has been a consequent failure of justice. The earlier contrary Supreme Court Decision rendered in the case ofChandrika Misir vs. Bhaiya Lal, AIR 1973 SC 2391 remains no longer relevant law on the subject in view of the newly added section 331 (1-A). The plea of want of jurisdiction can thus be raised before the appellate or revisional courts only if the two conditions, noted below, are fulfilled :
(1) That the objection regarding want of jurisdiction was taken in the court of first instance.
(2) There has been a consequent failure of justice. Parashuram Tewari vs. Bhanu Pratap Tewari, 1974 RD 176 (All) see also, 1978 ALJ 316 (DB)

sections.title: 41. Injunction lie in Civil Court with respect of agricultural land
sections.content: The jurisdiction of the Civil Court is only ousted by virtue of Section 331 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950. Under it the jurisdiction of the Civil Court is only excluded in case it falls under Col. 4 or under Col. 3 of Schedule II. So far as proceeding for cancellation of the Bhumidari is concerned, it is a matter covered under Section 137-A of the said Act, which is not referred in Col. 3 of the said Schedule. This apart, ouster of Civil Court jurisdiction under the said Act would only arise if defendant could be a tenant under the said Act or in other words there existed such basic fact, before coming in force of the said Act, to qualify him to be such. We find the finding recorded is that the appellant was not even in cultivatory possession over the land in dispute prior to the coming of the said Act. The Bhumidari Sanad was granted in view of his being wrongly recorded as Sirdar. Once the basic fact is recorded by Courts below that he was not in cultivatory possession prior to the Act. Question of any entry as Sirdar cannot stand and for adjudicating this the Civil Court jurisdiction is not ousted.Vithalbhai (P) Ltd. vs. Union Bank of India, (2005) 4 SCC 315 see also Samar Singh vs. Kedar Nath, 1987 Suppl. SCC 663

sections.title: 42. Demolition and joint possession—injunction suit
sections.content: The civil court, and no other court, had the power to grant the relief for injunction, demolition and joint possession provided the same was considered to be an equitable-relief. Where it could not be considered to be an equitable relief the suit would fall not because the civil court had no jurisdiction to entertain it but because it did not consider that the relief prayed for was an equitable relief.Ram Awalamb vs. Jata Shanker, 1968 RD 470 (All)(FB)

sections.title: 43. Civil suit when not barred u/s 331
sections.content: Under Section 331, jurisdiction of civil court is expressly barred for the suits mentioned in Column 3 of Schedule II of U.P. Act No. 1 of 1951 and impliedly barred for a suit based on a cause of action, in respect of which, relief could be obtained by revenue court (mentioned in column 4 of Schedule II). Column 3 of Schedule II of U.P. Act No. 1 of 1951 does not provide for a suit for cancellation of sale deed of agricultural land as such Section 331 (1) does not expressly bar a suit for cancellation of sale deeds.Chandrika vs. Shivnath on 24 May, 2016 see also Smt. Bismillah vs. Janeshwar Prasad, AIR 1990 SC 540

sections.title: 44. Grove land and injunction
sections.content: Once a finding has been given that the land was a grove and was not an abadi, no suit for injunction could have been filed in a civil court and the court below should have relegated the plaintiffs to seek an appropriate relief before the revenue court.Bauram vs. Munni, 2008 (2) AWC 1336: 2008 (26) LCD 1220 (All)

sections.title: 45. Injunction suit regarding house, sahan, ghera, sariya, well, trees etc
sections.content: Suit for permanent injunction with respect to houses, sahan, ghera, sariya, well and trees on plot is not barred under Section 330 and 331. Such suit cannot be thrown away by civil court because revenue court can not grant relief in respect of house etc. The fact of entry of the name into revenue records on the basis of compromise filed by impostor can be proved by leading evidence and that exercise can only be done by Civil Court. Civil court will have jurisdiction in such suit.Smt. Lakhpata vs. 2nd ADJ, Faizabad, 1998 (4) AWC 696 (All)(LB)

sections.title: 46. Declaration of title over agricultural land
sections.content: If the name of the plaintiff is not recorded in revenue records as tenure holder of the agricultural land and the question of declaration of title is involved, the jurisdiction of the civil court in relation to such agricultural land would be barred u/s 331 of the UPZA & LR Act 1950 as the revenue court would have exclusive jurisdiction under section 229-B of the act to declare the title over the agricultural land. Smt. Shail Kumari vs. Abhilakh, 1998 RD 272 (All)

sections.title: 47. Declaratory suit not barred by Sec. 331
sections.content: It is not every suit of declaration that is barred under Section 331, the categories of declaration which cannot be granted by a civil court are those mentioned against Serial No. 34 and they are of the types specified in Sections 229, 229-B and 229-C of the Act. The only ground on which the suit was held to be barred was that the appellants were asamis and their ejectment could not be granted by the civil court. A finding recorded by the civil court on the question of jurisdictional fact is binding on the parties to the suit. Kali Prasad vs. DDC, 2000 (91) RD 549 (SC)

sections.title: 48. Banjar land
sections.content: Land was recorded as banjar land and was not declared an abadi land under Section 143 of the Act, cannot be treated as abadi land. Mere existence of certain constructions over a Bhumidhari land would not take it out of purview of the provisions of Act unless a declaration is made under Section 143. Basti Ram vs. Nagar Nigam, Ghaziabad, 1999 (4) AWC 3041: 2000 (18) LCD 138 (All) see also Indrajeet Singh vs. Arjun Singh, 1983 ALJ 388 (All) and Shiv Prasad vs. Thakur Prasad, 1986 RD 253 (All)

sections.title: 49. Declaration under Section 143
sections.content: The land does not cease to be an agricultural land until a declaration under Section 143 is given by the Revenue Court and therefore, the Court is bound to refer to the revenue court under Section 331A of the Act.Magnu Ahir vs. Mahabir, 1988 RD 301: 1981 (7) ALR 308 (All)

sections.title: 50. Change of user
sections.content: Construction of a boundary wall over a particular portion of land will not change the nature of land. It will not cease to be bhumidhari land unless the user is changed. Under Section 143 of the Act It is only where a bhumidhar with transferable rights uses his holding or part thereof for a purpose not connected with agriculture, horticulture or animal husbandry that the land can be declared being used for such purpose and it will cease to be bhumidhari but unless a land is put to such a use, no such declaration under Section 143 can be made under said provisions. Smt. Urmila Devi vs. Pooran Chand Dabar, 1999 (17) LCD 201 (All)(D.B.)

sections.title: 51. Cancellation of sale deed—Plaintiff not recorded tenure holder
sections.content: Where a recorded tenure holder having a prima facie title and in possession, files suit in the Civil Court for cancellation of sale deed having obtained on the ground of fraud or impersonation cannot be directed to file a suit for declaration in the revenue Court, reason being that in such a case, prima facie, the title of the recorded tenure holder is not under cloud. He does not require declaration of his title to the land. The position would be different where a person not being a recorded tenure holder seeks cancellation of sale deed by filing a suit in the civil court on the ground of fraud or impersonation. There necessarily the plaintiff is required to seek a declaration of his title and, therefore, he may be directed to approach the revenue Court, as the sale deed being void has to be ignored for giving him relief for declaration and possession. Shri Ram vs. 1st ADJ, 2001 (19) LCD 740 (SC), Khamani Ram vs. District Judge, Budaun, 1983 ALJ 1378 (All)

sections.title: 52. Cancellation of Will
sections.content: The principal and in fact the only relief sought in the suit filed before Civil Court is for cancellation of alleged Will with respect to the property in question. No relief has been sought with respect to the rights and title of a tenure holder or declaration of title or status. Held, since the relief sought in the original suit is for cancellation of the alleged will, it cannot be said that the suit was not maintainable before the Civil Court and also that it was not necessary for the plaintiff to file suit for declaration of title under Section 229-B. Suit not barred by Section 331. Manoj Kumar vs. District Judge, Jaunpur, 2011 (29) LCD 2480 (All)

sections.title: 53. Gift deed and sale deed—Suit for cancellation
sections.content: In the present case, there are two main questions-one is whether the gift-deed and sale-deed are voidable on the basis of the allegations contained in the plaint, namely, fraud in obtaining the deeds. The documents were not duly executed by the vendor. They did not contain his signatures and was without consideration and the second question is whether the plaintiff-respondent was born prior to the enforcement of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act. If he was born prior to the enforcement of the Act, he will have right over the sir land in question. In view of the allegations contained in the suit for the cancellation of the documents, the suit is maintainable in the civil court. Smt. Kalindi vs. ADJ, Deoria, 2001 (19) LCD 1046 (All)

sections.title: 54. Compromise decree—Suit for cancellation of
sections.content: Where in a declaratory suit filed u/s 229-B of the UPZA & LR Act, 1950, a compromise was entered into on behalf of minor through guardian and compromise decree was passed, it has been held that though the compromise was neither void or voidable under the Contract Act but still the minor on attaining majority can allege that his interest suffered prejudice and may ask for cancellation of the compromise decree and such suit would be maintainable in the civil court. Dilraj Yadav vs. IIIrd ADJ, Azamgarh, 1998 (3) AWC 1699 (All)

sections.title: 55. Stay order—Effect of
sections.content: It is settled principle that the stay of an order does not wipe out the effect of an order (Shree Chamundi Mopeds Ltd. vs. Church of South India Trust Assn, 1992 AIR 1439),thus, the entry in favour of plaintiff as on the date of filing of the suit in December, 1996 was intact and had not been set aside. In the aforesaid background suit for cancellation of sale deed before the civil court was maintainable. Smt.Brijbala vs. Additional District Judge And ... on 21 November, 2012

sections.title: 56. Khasra entries—proof of title
sections.content: Khasra entries are not proof of title and ownership of land. Municipal Corporation, Gwalior vs. Puran Singh, (2015) 5 SCC 725

sections.title: 57. Events pendentelite not to oust jurisdiction of the Civil Court
sections.content: A party who is defeated on the merits of the dispute may not by securing an order from another Court during the pendency of a, suit be permitted to displace the jurisdiction of the Civil Court to, try the suit which was within its competence when the suit was filed.Smt. Sonawati vs. Shri Ram, AIR 1968 SC 466

sections.title: 58. Partition & injunction with respect of abadi or house
sections.content: The Court below after perusing the record of the case, came to the conclusion that the property in dispute was either houses or abadi land and it was recorded in revenue papers as abadi and makan. The said finding is based on relevant evidence on the record and does not suffer from any jurisdictional error. The Court below was right in holding that the civil court had the jurisdiction to entertain and decide the suit.Lakshmi Prasad vs. Smt. Krishna Devi, 2000 (91) RD 372 (All) 20, referred and relied on 1991 AWC 431 and 1980 ALJ 184

sections.title: 59. Correction in Revenue Records
sections.content: In view of the provisions under Section 331 the civil court can not direct for correction or expunction of entries in revenue records and same can be done only by the revenue courts. Kamla Shankar vs. IIIrd ADJ Mirzapur, 1998 (89) R.D. 484 (All), Magan Lal Chaturvedi vs. District Judge, 1998 ALJ 2323, Deokinandan vs. Surajpal, 1996 ALJ 144 (SC), Tej Bhan Singh vs. II ADJ Jaunpur, 1995 ALJ 109, Surya Narayan Pandey vs. Addl Civil Judge, Gyanpur, 1995 RD (H) 50, Jyoti Ram vs. District Judge, 1995 RD 99, Tej Bhan Singh vs. IX ADJ, Jaunpur, 1994 RD 476, Indra Pal vs. Jagannath, 1993 ALJ 235, Bhagwat Prasad vs. Jitendra Narain, 1991 ALJ 971, Chandra Deo Pathak vs. Swami Nath Pathak, 1987 RD 51, Vijai Singh vs. 2nd ADJ Bulandshahar, 1982 ALJ 725, Jai Singh vs. Hanumant Singh, 1979 ALJ 645, Kishori Lal vs. Shambhoo Nath, 1978 ALJ 1273, Parsottam vs. Narottam, 1970 ALJ 505 (All) (DB)

sections.title: 60. Tenancy rights
sections.content: Rights of tenancy are determinable by Revenue Authorities; in a case where sale deed is being questioned on basis of fraud, the executor of sale deed must be necessarily impleaded and whether the matter can be decided by Revenue Court or Civil Court, would depend upon pleadings taken in plaint and relief sought in the suit.Azhar Hasan vs. District Judge, Saharanpur, AIR 1998 SC 2960: JT 1998 (4) SC 313: (1998) 3 SCC 246: 1998 ALJ 2008 (SC)

sections.title: 209. Bar against certain appeals
1. ‘Affected parties’—connotation of
sections.content: Merely for the reason that the private respondents were not made a party to the proceedings despite being tenure holders of the adjoining plots, cannot lead to the conclusion that they would not be ‘affected parties’ or would not be covered within the meaning of the expression ‘party aggrieved’, so as to seek recall of the order passed ex- parte. Hence application for recall of order is maintainable. Tarkeshwar and others vs. State of U.P. and others, 2023 AIR CC 2513 (All)

sections.title: 2. Scope of
sections.content: A ‘review on merits’ is permissible only in case the forum in question is vested with the power of review by the statute; however, the power to grant ‘procedural review’ is inherent. Kapra Mazdoor Ekta Union vs. Birla Cotton Spinning and Weaving Mills Ltd., (2005) 13 SCC 777

sections.title: 210. Power to call for the records
sections.content:
(1) The Board or the Commissioner may call for the record of any suit or proceeding decided by any subordinate revenue Court in which no appeal lies, 167[* * *], for the purpose of satisfying itself or himself as to the legality or propriety of any order passed in such suit or proceeding; and if such subordinate Court appeals to have
167 Omitted “or where an appeal lies but has not been preferred” vide U.P. Act No. 4 of 2016 w.e.f. 16.12.2015
(a) exercised a jurisdiction not vested in it by law; or
(b) failed to exercise a jurisdiction so vested; or
(c) acted in the exercise of such jurisdiction illegally or with material irregularity;
the Board, or the Commissioner, as the case may be, may pass such order in the case as it or he thinks fit.
(2) If an application under this section has been moved by any person either to the Board or to the Commissioner, no further application by the same person shall be entertained by the other of them.
168[Explanation
168 Inserted vide U.P. Act No. 4 of 2016 w.e.f. 16.12.2015
For the removal of doubt it is, hereby, declared that when an application under this section has been moved either to the Board or to the Commissioner, the application shall not be permitted to be withdrawn for the purpose of filing the application against the same order to the other of them.]
(3) No application under this section shall be entertained after the expiry of a period of 169[sixty days] from the date of the order sought to be revised or from the date of commencement of this Code, whichever is later.
169 Substituted vide U.P. Act No. 4 of 2016 w.e.f. 16.12.2015
